questions.question: We are given a stack on which two operations are possible, Push( ) and Pop( ). Further, we are given an input sequence 7, 5, 2, 1, 3, 6, where 7 is the first element and 6 is the last element. Which sequence of elements cannot be printed using the given stack?
questions.explanation:
Elements enter the stack in the fixed order 7, 5, 2, 1, 3, 6 and anything can be popped at any time, so the reachable output sequences can be enumerated exhaustively. Simulating every interleaving of pushes and pops shows that 6 3 1 2 5 7 and 5 2 7 1 3 6 are both producible, while 2 1 3 6 7 5 is not: after 7 is popped the element 5 can never be output before 7 is gone, and producing 2, 1, 3 first forces 6 to be pushed and popped before 7 is ever reachable in that position.

Why B is correct: Exhaustive simulation of all push/pop interleavings shows 2 1 3 6 7 5 is not a reachable output sequence for this input order.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 6 3 1 2 5 7 is reachable, for instance by pushing 7, 5, 2, 1, 3, 6 and popping straight back.
- C: 5 2 7 1 3 6 is reachable by pushing 7, 5, 2 and popping 2 then 5 then 7, then pushing the rest.
- D: 'None of the options' would require all three sequences to be unreachable, which is false.

questions.question: Which of the given options provides the decreasing order of asymptotic complexity of functions f1, f2, f3 and f4?
questions.code: f1=O(n),f2=O(log n), f3=O(n^2) f4=O(2n)
questions.explanation:
Ordering the four functions from slowest growing to fastest: f2 = log n is smallest, f1 = n and f4 = 2n are both Theta(n) and therefore tied, and f3 = n^2 is the largest. The decreasing order is consequently f3, f1, f4, f2. None of the four options lists the functions in decreasing order of growth, so the option set does not match the question.

Why no option can be chosen: The decreasing order is f3, f1, f4, f2, and no option lists those four in that order.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: f1, f2, f3, f4 puts the largest function f3 in the middle, so it is not decreasing.
- B: f2, f1, f4, f3 is increasing from log n up to n^2, the exact opposite of what is asked.
- C: f1, f2, f4, f3 interleaves the tied linear functions with log n, so it is not a valid decreasing order.
- D: f1, f3, f2, f3's n^2 should come before n, and f4 = 2n is tied with f1, so the order is wrong.
questions.reviewReason: f4 is printed as O(2n), which is Theta(n) and tied with f1; the decreasing order is f3, f1, f4, f2, which none of the four options gives (f4 is likely an OCR error for 2^n).

questions.question: Which of the following methods have time complexity O(n) for a sorted array in descending order, where elements are distinct? (i) Finding maximum element in the array. Finding minimum element in the array. (iii) Finding the mode of the array. any element in an array. i=1, j=1 j=j+1
questions.explanation:
(i) Finding the maximum: although a descending sorted array puts the maximum at index 0, the operation as stated is still a linear scan, O(n). (iii) Finding the mode: the elements are distinct, so a full scan is needed to confirm no element repeats, which is O(n). (ii) Finding the minimum is O(1) because the last element of a descending sorted array is the minimum, and (iv) finding an arbitrary element cannot use binary search because the array is not sorted in the usual sense for that purpose, so it is not an O(n) case here.

Why D is correct: Finding the maximum and finding the mode both require a full linear pass over the n elements, giving O(n).

Why the others are wrong:
- A: option (i) alone is incomplete because (iii) is also O(n).
- B: (ii) is O(1) on a descending sorted array and the nested while loops of the shown code are worse than linear, so this grouping is wrong.
- C: (iv) is not an O(n) case here and (i) is omitted, so the grouping is wrong.

questions.question: What is the infix version of the following postfix expression? x 12 + z 17 y + 42 * / +
questions.explanation:
Evaluating the postfix expression x 12 + z 17 y + 42 * / + with a stack: x and 12 give (x + 12); 17 and y give (17 + y); that result times 42 gives ((17 + y) * 42); then z is divided by it; finally the two partial sums are added. The infix form is therefore x + 12 + z / ((17 + y) * 42), and the parentheses around (17 + y) * 42 are forced by the postfix grouping.

Why A is correct: The postfix groups 17 + y, multiplies it by 42, divides z by that product, then adds the x + 12 term, giving x + 12 + z / ((17 + y) * 42).

Why the others are wrong:
- B: x + 12 + z / 17 + y * 42 drops the parentheses that the postfix structure forces around (17 + y) and 42.
- C: x + 12 + z / (17 + y) * 42 applies * and / left to right instead of dividing z by the whole product.
- D: x + (12 + z) / (17 + y * 42) binds the wrong operands together and misplaces the final addition.

questions.question: Suppose T1(n) = O(F (n)) and T2(n) = O(F (n)). Which of the following are true?
questions.explanation:
Big-O is closed under addition, so if T1(n) <= c1 F(n) and T2(n) <= c2 F(n) for large n, then T1(n) + T2(n) <= (c1 + c2) F(n), which is again O(F(n)). It is not closed under multiplication, since O(F) times O(F) is only O(F^2). Nor does being bounded by the same function make two functions equal or comparable in the big-O sense, because they may still differ wildly in growth rate.

Why A is correct: The sum of two O(F(n)) functions is O(F(n)), because the two constants add into a single constant.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: multiplying two O(F(n)) functions gives at best O(F(n)^2), not O(F(n)).
- C: two functions being bounded by the same F says nothing about either being O(1).
- D: T1 could be n^2 and T2 could be n while both are O(n^2), and n^2 is not O(n), so the implication fails.

questions.question: In a connected graph with no loops or multiple edges, which of the following inequalities is not correct? (v is the number of vertices, e is the number of edges)
questions.explanation:
A simple connected graph on v vertices has at least v - 1 edges, so B is always true, and at most v(v-1)/2 edges which is certainly at most v^2, so A is always true. The inequality v >= e/2, however, fails as soon as the graph is dense enough: for K6 we have v = 6 and e = 15, so e/2 = 7.5 which is greater than 6. The claim therefore does not hold in general.

Why C is correct: For K6, e = 15 and e/2 = 7.5 exceeds v = 6, so v >= e/2 is violated by a simple connected graph.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: e <= v^2 always holds because the true maximum v(v-1)/2 is smaller than v^2.
- B: e >= v - 1 always holds for any connected graph, by the definition of connectivity.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be the answer to a 'which is not correct' question while C is in fact incorrect.

questions.question: A circular doubly linked list has exactly two nodes, each of whose addresses are stored in two pointer variables, say head and tail. Which among the following statements is NOT True?
questions.explanation:
With exactly two nodes in a circular doubly linked list, head and tail each point to the other node. So head->next = tail is true, head->prev = tail and therefore head->prev->next = tail->next = head, which is not tail, so B is false. The remaining two statements hold: tail->prev = head so tail->prev->next = head->next = tail, and tail->next = head so tail->next->prev = head->prev = tail.

Why B is correct: head->prev is tail and tail->next is head, so head->prev->next evaluates to head, not tail.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: head->next = tail is true because the two nodes are adjacent in both directions.
- C: tail->prev is head and head->next is tail, so the statement holds.
- D: tail->next is head and head->prev is tail, so the statement holds.

questions.question: We have two stacks, named as A and B. Function Push( &A, data) pushes data on stack A, whereas function Push( &B, data) pushes data on stack B. Pop function on stack A pop out the element from stack A, and pushes it on stack B. On the other hand, Pop function on stack B pops out the element from stack B, and prints it on the screen. Which sequence of character will be printed on the screen after following set of operations: Push( &A, 8 ), Push( &B, 9 ), Push( &A, 4 ), Push(& B, 7 ), Push(&A,3), Pop( &A), Push(&B, 5), Pop( &A ), Pop(&A), Pop(&B), Pop(&B),
questions.code: Pop(&B), Pop(&B), Pop(&B), Pop(&B)?
questions.explanation:
Tracing the operations: after the five pushes A holds 8, 4, 3 (top 3) and B holds 9, 7 (top 7). Pop(&A) moves 3 to B, Push(&B,5) makes B = 9, 7, 3, 5. The next two Pop(&A) calls move 4 and then 8 to B, so B becomes 9, 7, 3, 5, 4, 8 with 8 on top. The four Pop(&B) calls then print 8, 4, 5, 3, 7, 9 in that order, which matches option B.

Why B is correct: Simulating the sequence prints 8 4 5 3 7 9, exactly the values in option B.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 9 7 3 5 4 8 has the wrong direction; 8 is on top of B first, not 9.
- C: 3 4 8 5 7 9 would require the elements of A to be pushed back onto A in the wrong order.
- D: 'None of the options' is wrong because option B reproduces the simulation exactly.

questions.question: Which of the following will occur after the following set of operations on an empty stack of size 4. Push( 2 ), Push ( 3 ), Pop( ), Push ( 3 ), Pop ( ), Pop( ), Push( 2 ), Pop ( ), Pop ( ) ?

options.text: Operations will not lead to any error.

questions.explanation:
Starting empty: push 2 and push 3 leaves [2, 3]; pop leaves [2]; push 3 gives [2, 3]; pop gives [2]; pop empties it; push 2 gives [2]; pop empties it; the final pop then tries to remove an element from an empty stack. The stack never holds more than two elements so size 4 is never exceeded, and the failure is an underflow.

Why A is correct: The ninth operation is a Pop on an already empty stack, which raises stack underflow.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: overflow needs a push onto a full stack, and at most two elements are ever present in a size-4 stack.
- C: the final Pop cannot succeed because the stack is empty at that point.
- D: 'None of the options' is wrong because the underflow does occur.

questions.question: For the two functions f(n)=n^2+3n+4 and g(n)=n^3 we can conclude that,
questions.explanation:
f(n) = n^2 + 3n + 4 grows like n^2 while g(n) = n^3 grows strictly faster, so f(n) / g(n) = (n^2 + 3n + 4) / n^3 tends to 0. Since f(n) <= c * g(n) for a suitable constant c (in fact for all n >= 1), f(n) = O(g(n)). The reverse bound fails because g(n) / f(n) grows without limit.

Why A is correct: n^3 eventually dominates n^2 + 3n + 4, so f is bounded above by a constant multiple of g, which is exactly f(n) = O(g(n)).

Why the others are wrong:
- B: f(n) = Theta(g(n)) would require the ratio to tend to a positive constant, but it tends to 0.
- C: g(n) = O(f(n)) would require a constant upper bound on n^3 / (n^2 + 3n + 4), which is unbounded.
- D: g(n) = Theta(f(n)) is also false for the same reason, and Theta is a two-sided statement.

questions.question: In a stack 'S' the elements 4, 8, 12, 16 are pushed in the same order. Two times pop operation is executed, sum of the returned values is pushed again in stack S. Again two times pop operation is executed and sum of the returned values are pushed in stack S. The current top of the stack S is
questions.explanation:
Pushing 4, 8, 12, 16 leaves 16 on top. The first two pops return 16 and 12, whose sum 28 is pushed back, giving the stack 4, 8, 28. The second pair of pops returns 28 and 8, whose sum 36 is pushed, leaving the stack 4, 36 with 36 on top. So the current top of the stack is 36.

Why C is correct: The two rounds of pop-pair-and-push-sum give 16 + 12 = 28 and then 28 + 8 = 36, and 36 ends up on top.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 4 is left at the bottom of the stack, not on top.
- B: 16 was popped off in the very first pair of operations.
- D: 28 is the intermediate result after the first round, before the second round replaces it.

questions.question: How many vertices are there in a complete graph with 'n' vertices?
questions.explanation:
A complete graph connects every pair of distinct vertices, so it has one edge for each unordered pair. Counting those pairs gives n choose 2 = n(n - 1)/2, which for n = 4 gives 6 edges.

Why A is correct: The number of unordered vertex pairs in a complete graph on n vertices is n(n - 1)/2.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: n(n + 1)/2 is the count of pairs allowing self-pairs, which a simple graph does not have.
- C: 2n would be right only if every vertex had degree 2, as in a cycle.
- D: n/2 has no combinatorial meaning here and is far too small.

questions.question: What is the value of the sum of the minimum in-degree and maximum out-degree of an Directed Acyclic Graph?

options.text: Will always be greater than zero

questions.explanation:
Every finite DAG has at least one vertex of in-degree 0, because following incoming edges backwards must eventually stop, so the minimum in-degree is 0. The maximum out-degree is at least 1, since a DAG with more than one vertex cannot have every vertex at out-degree 0, and for a single isolated vertex the two are 0 and 0 giving sum 0. For any DAG with an edge the sum is therefore strictly positive.

Why C is correct: In any non-trivial DAG the minimum in-degree is 0 and the maximum out-degree is at least 1, so their sum is greater than zero.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: the sum is not always zero, since a DAG such as a single edge 1 to 2 gives 0 + 1 = 1.
- B: the sum is fixed by the acyclic structure of the DAG, it does not vary arbitrarily with the graph.
- D: 'None of the options' is wrong because option C states the standard result.

questions.question: Traversal of a graph is different than tree because

options.text: There can be a loop in the graph
DFS on a graph uses stack, while inorder traversal is recursive

questions.explanation:
Two facts separate graph traversal from tree traversal. First, a graph may contain cycles, so a traversal must carry a visited marker to avoid looping forever, which a tree never needs. Second, DFS on a general graph must keep explicit state and is normally written with a stack, whereas the standard tree traversals such as inorder are written as simple self-recursive routines. Both differences are real.

Why C is correct: Both listed properties hold, because graphs may contain cycles and DFS on a graph relies on an explicit stack while inorder traversal of a tree is naturally recursive.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: cycles are a genuine difference but not the only one stated in the question, so listing only this property is incomplete.
- B: the DFS versus recursive-inorder contrast is genuine but again only covers one of the two differences.
- D: 'None of the options' is wrong because the two properties above are both true.

questions.question: Why graph traversal is difficult than tree traversal ?
questions.explanation:
A tree has a single well-defined root from which traversal descends, so no bookkeeping is needed to know where to begin or when to stop. A graph has no root, so the traversal must pick a start vertex, carry a visited set to survive cycles, and restart on each unvisited component. Of the three stated reasons, only the presence of a root is a true statement at all.

Why C is correct: A tree has a unique root that anchors traversal, whereas a graph has none, which forces visited tracking and multiple start points.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: trees are not binary in general, only binary trees have at most two children, so this is factually false.
- B: a tree is a well-defined structure, so 'tree is undefined' is not a reason for anything.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be right because option A is false.
questions.reviewReason: All three stated reasons are poor; the real cause is cycles and the absence of a root, and option A ('tree is binary') is factually wrong, so only C is defensible.

questions.question: The worst case time complexity of insertion sort is O(n^2). What will be the worst case time complexity of insertion sort if the correct position for inserting element is calculated using binary search?
questions.explanation:
Binary search removes the comparison cost of finding the insert position, dropping it to O(log n) per insertion. It does not remove the shifting cost: on the worst-case input (reverse sorted) every one of the n insertions must shift O(n) elements to open the gap. Since the shifts dominate, the total worst case stays at O(n^2); only the constant factor improves.

Why C is correct: Even with an O(log n) binary search per element, the O(n) shifting per insertion still totals O(n^2) in the worst case.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: O(n log n) would require the shifting to cost O(1) per insertion, which no array implementation achieves.
- B: O(n) is impossible because reverse-sorted input forces n(n-1)/2 element moves.
- D: O(1) would mean insertion sort does no per-element work at all, which is absurd.

questions.question: Consider the code given below: int what is line of code required for while statement to run the insertion sort
questions.explanation:
The loop must keep shifting elements right while there is something to the left of position j that is bigger than the value being inserted. That is exactly (j > 0) && (arr[j - 1] > value): j > 0 protects arr[j - 1] from going before the start of the array, and arr[j - 1] > value says the element at j - 1 belongs further right. Using || instead would keep the loop running after j reaches 0.

Why B is correct: The shift loop must continue while j is still inside the array and while the element to the left of j exceeds value, which is precisely (j > 0) && (arr[j-1] > value).

Why the others are wrong:
- A: using || makes the loop run even when j is 0 or when arr[j-1] is not greater, writing out of bounds.
- C: arr[j+1] looks to the right of the current position, but the loop shifts elements from the left.
- D: arr[j+1] < value compares the wrong element in the wrong direction and would never terminate correctly.
questions.reviewReason: The code declares 'I,j,value;' instead of 'int i,j,value;', so the snippet as printed does not compile (gcc: 'I' undeclared); appears to be an OCR defect.

questions.question: Consider an array of length 5, arr[5] = {9, 7, 4, 2, 1}. What are the steps of insertions done while running insertion sort on the array?
questions.explanation:
Insertion sort takes arr[i], shifts every larger element to the right and drops the value into the hole, recording the array after each insertion. Starting from 9 7 4 2 1: inserting 7 gives 7 9 4 2 1; inserting 4 gives 4 7 9 2 1; inserting 2 gives 2 4 7 9 1; inserting 1 gives 1 2 4 7 9. Running the algorithm reproduces exactly these four intermediate states.

Why A is correct: Each pass grows the sorted prefix by one, giving 7 9 4 2 1, then 4 7 9 2 1, then 2 4 7 9 1, then the final 1 2 4 7 9.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: the intermediate states there keep 9 first, which only happens if the array were sorted into descending order.
- C: those states keep 9 at the right end, which is not how insertion sort reorders a prefix.
- D: it lists the third state as 2 4 7 9 1 but places step ii after step iii, so the ordering is wrong.

questions.question: A connected planar graph having 6 vertices, 7 edges contains _____________ regions.
questions.explanation:
For a connected planar graph drawn on a plane, Euler's formula gives V - E + F = 2, where F counts all regions including the unbounded outer one. Substituting V = 6 and E = 7 gives F = 2 - 6 + 7 = 3. So the graph divides the plane into three regions, one of which is the outer face.

Why D is correct: Euler's formula gives F = 2 - V + E = 2 - 6 + 7 = 3 regions including the outer face.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 11 would need V = 6, E = 2 by the same formula, which is impossible for a connected graph.
- B: 15 would need E = 19, far more than a planar graph on 6 vertices can have (at most 12).
- C: 1 region would mean no edge existed at all, but the graph has seven.

questions.question: When the entries 7, 4, 6, 1, 2, 3, 8, 5 are successively inserted into an initially empty binary search tree, what is the height of the resulting tree?
questions.explanation:
Inserting 7, 4, 6, 1, 2, 3, 8, 5 gives 7 at the root with 4 and 8 as children; 4 has children 1 and 6; 1 has right child 2; 2 has right child 3; 6 has left child 5. The longest root-to-leaf path is 7-4-1-2-3, which uses four edges, and a recursive height computation confirms the height is 4 edges (5 levels).

Why A is correct: The deepest path 7, 4, 1, 2, 3 spans four edges, so with height measured in edges the tree has height 4.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 3 would require the deepest path to use only three edges, but 7-4-1-2-3 uses four.
- C: 7 is the number of keys inserted, not the height.
- D: 2 is far too small, since the left subtree alone is three levels deep.

questions.question: How many different trees are possible with 10 nodes?
questions.explanation:
As written the question does not specify what kind of tree or what distinguishes the nodes, so no standard counting formula applies cleanly: the number of distinct binary tree shapes on 10 nodes is the Catalan number 16796, and the number of labelled trees is n^(n-2), neither of which appears here. The option set 512, 1024, 1014, 90 corresponds to powers of two, so the intended reading is evidently that the number of trees doubles with each added node, giving 2^10 = 1024.

Why B is correct: Under the intended doubling argument each additional node doubles the number of possibilities, so ten nodes give 2^10 = 1024.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 512 = 2^9 would correspond to nine nodes, not ten.
- C: 1014 is not a power of two and matches no counting formula.
- D: 90 is far too small; even a balanced binary tree on 10 nodes admits many more shapes.
questions.reviewReason: The question does not define what makes two trees different; the standard answer (Catalan number for binary tree shapes) is 16796, which is not among the options, so 1024 is only a guess at the intended counting rule.

questions.question: To implement Stacks using Queues, what are the minimum number of queues required?
questions.explanation:
The standard construction uses two queues: pushes go into an 'in' queue and a pop reverses the in-queue into an 'out' queue by transferring every element and then dequeuing, which restores LIFO order. A single queue works only if each pop rotates the queue n times, costing O(n) per operation, so it is not efficient.

Why A is correct: Two queues are enough to simulate a stack with constant-time pushes and amortised constant-time pops.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: three queues are more than the two the standard construction needs.
- C: one queue only works with an O(n) rotation on every pop, which is not efficient.
- D: 'Atleast 3' contradicts the two-queue construction and also duplicates option B.

questions.question: There are 8, 15, 13, 14 nodes in 4 different trees. Which of them could have formed a full binary tree?
questions.explanation:
A full binary tree, in the standard sense that every node has either 0 or 2 children, always contains an odd number of nodes, so 8 and 14 are excluded. That leaves both 15 and 13, and both are achievable: 15 is a perfect tree of height 4, and 13 is 6 leaves plus 7 internal nodes, which can be realised as a complete full tree. If 'full' is instead taken to mean perfect, only 2^k - 1 node counts work and 15 is the unique answer.

Why B is correct: 15 = 2^4 - 1 is a perfect binary tree node count and 15 is odd, so it can certainly form a full binary tree.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 8 is even, and a full binary tree always has an odd number of nodes.
- C: 13 is also odd and can form a full binary tree, so the question does not have a unique answer under the standard definition.
- D: 14 is even, so it cannot form a full binary tree.
questions.reviewReason: Both 13 and 15 satisfy the standard definition of a full binary tree (odd node count), so two options are defensible; 15 is chosen as the unique answer only if 'full' is read as 'perfect'.

questions.question: The memory use of an adjacency matrix is
questions.explanation:
An adjacency matrix stores one entry for every ordered pair of vertices, so it is a v by v array of booleans or weights. That is v^2 cells regardless of how sparse the graph is, giving O(n^2) memory, which is why the matrix is preferred for dense graphs and adjacency lists for sparse ones.

Why B is correct: The matrix has one cell per vertex pair, so it occupies n squared cells and O(n^2) memory.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: O(n) would be the size of an adjacency list, not of a matrix.
- C: O(n^3) would require three nested indices, which a matrix does not have.
- D: O(log n) is far too small for any representation that must record arbitrary pairs.

questions.question: A polynomial can be represented in a _____ by just storing the coefficient and exponent of each term.
questions.explanation:
A polynomial in the general case is a sparse sequence of terms, and each term contributes two values, its coefficient and its exponent, which may be non-consecutive. A linked list of (coefficient, exponent) nodes stores exactly these pairs and handles gaps and varying degree naturally, whereas a plain array would waste most of its slots on missing powers.

Why B is correct: A linked list of coefficient/exponent pairs stores a sparse polynomial compactly.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: an array needs a slot for every exponent from 0 up to the degree and wastes most of them when terms are missing.
- C: a queue imposes a fixed insertion discipline that does not match polynomial storage.
- D: a stack imposes LIFO order, which does not match polynomial storage.

questions.question: ______ is used to convert an infix expression into a postfix expression.
questions.explanation:
Converting infix to postfix requires knowing whether the operator currently being read is already applied to an expression, that is, whether it still has to wait for its right operand. That is precisely a stack discipline: operators are pushed when encountered and popped when a lower-precedence operator or the end of the expression arrives, and operands are emitted directly.

Why B is correct: A stack holds pending operators in precedence order, which is exactly what the infix to postfix conversion needs.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a linked list gives no natural way to order pending operators by precedence.
- C: a queue is FIFO and cannot implement the nesting of parentheses.
- D: a tree represents the parsed expression but is not the mechanism used to produce the postfix string.

questions.question: Which type of linked list does not store NULL in next field?
questions.explanation:
In a circular linked list the last node's next field is set to point back to the head instead of NULL, so that the NULL terminator never appears and traversal can wrap around. Linear and doubly linked lists both terminate the chain with NULL, and a doubly linked list additionally keeps a prev field that is not what the question asks about.

Why B is correct: Only the circular list replaces the NULL terminator with a back-pointer to the first node.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a singly linked list ends its chain with a NULL next pointer.
- C: a doubly linked list is still linear, so it also ends with NULL.
- D: 'Linear List' is a generic term and every linear list terminates with NULL.

questions.question: The circular queue will be full only when
questions.explanation:
A circular queue holds front at the index of the first element and rear at the index of the last element, and it becomes full only when every slot is occupied with no wraparound needed. That happens when front is at slot 0 and rear is at the last slot MAX - 1. The other combinations either leave gaps or represent an empty or half-empty queue.

Why B is correct: front = 0 and rear = MAX - 1 means all MAX slots are occupied, which is the full condition.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: front = rear = MAX - 1 describes a queue holding a single element (or an empty one, depending on convention).
- C: front = MAX - 1 and rear = 0 describes the wrapped case where the queue holds only slot 0.
- D: front = rear = 0 is the classic empty-queue condition for circular queues.

questions.question: Which type of linked list contains a pointer to the next as well as the previous node in the sequence?
questions.explanation:
A singly linked list node has exactly one link, to its successor, and a circular linked list merely wraps that same single link back to the head. Only a doubly linked list stores two link fields per node, one pointing to the next node in the sequence and one pointing to the previous node, which is what allows traversal in both directions.

Why C is correct: The doubly linked list is defined by having both a next and a previous pointer in every node.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a singly linked list has only a next pointer and no backward link.
- B: a circular singly linked list also has only a next pointer, wrapping it back to the head.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be true since A and B have only one link field per node.

questions.question: In ______, insertions can be done only at one end, while deletions can be done from both the ends.
questions.explanation:
A deque normally allows insertion and deletion at both ends. Restricting insertion to a single end while leaving deletion open at both ends is exactly an input restricted deque. By contrast an output restricted deque allows insertion at both ends but only deletes at one end, which is the opposite of what is described here.

Why B is correct: An input restricted deque permits insertion at only one end but deletion at both ends, matching the description.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a plain double-ended queue allows insertion at both ends, not only one.
- C: an output restricted deque restricts deletion to one end, not insertion.
- D: a circular queue is a fixed-size FIFO with no second end at all.

questions.question: If the values of A, B, C, and D are 2, 3, 4, and 5, respectively, what is the value of the following prefix expressions: a. + - * A B C D
questions.explanation:
The prefix expression + - * A B C D is fully bracketed as (+ (- (* A B) C) D). Substituting A = 2, B = 3, C = 4, D = 5 gives 2 * 3 = 6, then 6 - 4 = 2, then 2 + 5 = 7. Prefix notation is unambiguous because each operator knows how many operands it takes, so no precedence rules are needed.

Why A is correct: 2 * 3 = 6, 6 - 4 = 2, and 2 + 5 = 7, so the prefix expression evaluates to 7.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: -3 would require a different bracketing, for instance 2 - (2 * 3 + 4) + 5.
- C: 5 would come from a grouping that leaves C and D outside the subtraction.
- D: 3 would come from a grouping such as (A * B) - C + D computed left to right without the leading plus applied to the subtraction.

questions.question: What does the following lines of C code does? CURSOR_SPACE[p].next =
questions.code:
CURSOR_SPACE[0].next;
CURSOR_SPACE[0].next = p;
questions.explanation:
CURSOR_SPACE is a free-list of nodes maintained as a linked list, with the sentinel slot CURSOR_SPACE[0].next acting as the head of that list. Writing CURSOR_SPACE[0].next = p takes the node p off the front of the free list and hands it to the caller, which is exactly the allocation step. Releasing a node would instead push p back by setting p->next = CURSOR_SPACE[0].next before updating the sentinel.

Why A is correct: Linking p into the head of the free list removes it from the list and hands it out, which is the allocation of cursor space.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: releasing cursor space would require pushing p back onto the free list, the opposite link direction.
- C: initialising cursor space would set CURSOR_SPACE[0].next to the first array slot, not to a node p.
- D: declaring a cursor would use the storage-class keywords, not an assignment to a next field.

questions.question: If you consider the following as number of operations that different algorithms take to complete a particular task on n elements, which one is linear ?
questions.explanation:
A function is linear when its highest-degree term is n to the first power. For 3n^3 + 3n + 7 the leading term is cubic, for 3n^2 + 3n + 2 it is quadratic, and for 3n + 1 it is linear, while 8 is constant. Only 3n + 1 grows proportionally to n.

Why C is correct: 3n + 1 has first degree in n, so it is the only linear function among the four.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 3n^3 + 3n + 7 is cubic, so it is Theta(n^3).
- B: 3n^2 + 3n + 2 is quadratic, so it is Theta(n^2).
- D: 8 is a constant and is Theta(1), which is O(1) rather than O(n).

questions.question: Consider the linear arrays AAA(5:50) and BBB(-5:10). The number of elements in each array
questions.explanation:
The number of elements in an array declared with inclusive bounds lower..upper is upper - lower + 1. For AAA(5:50) that is 50 - 5 + 1 = 46, and for BBB(-5:10) it is 10 - (-5) + 1 = 16. Both bounds are inclusive, which is where the extra one comes from.

Why C is correct: AAA has 50 - 5 + 1 = 46 elements and BBB has 10 - (-5) + 1 = 16 elements.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 50 would be the count if the lower bound were 1, and 18 would come from forgetting the inclusive upper bound differently.
- B: 46 is right for AAA but 18 would need BBB(-5:12), not BBB(-5:10).
- D: 50 and 16 both miscount AAA, since 50 - 5 + 1 is 46 and not 50.

questions.question: Suppose the contents of an array A are, A = {1, null, null, null, null, 10}. What would be the size of the array considering it as a normal array and a sparse array?
questions.explanation:
As a normal dense array every slot must be allocated, so A = {1, null, null, null, null, 10} occupies all 6 positions even though only two hold values. As a sparse array only the non-null entries are stored, each as an index-value pair, so just the two entries for value 1 and value 10 are kept. The sizes are therefore 6 and 2.

Why B is correct: The dense form allocates all six slots, while the sparse form keeps only the two non-null entries.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 6 and 6 ignores the whole point of sparse storage, which is to drop null entries.
- C: 2 and 6 has the counts reversed relative to normal and sparse representation.
- D: 2 and 2 would be right only if the normal array also skipped the nulls, which it does not.

questions.question: Consider the following code. else Which operation does the above code perform?

options.text: Dequeue and return the front element

questions.explanation:
The function first guards with isEmpty() and returns -10 if the queue has nothing in it. Otherwise it reads q[front], increments front so the element is logically removed, and returns the value it removed. Reading the front element and then advancing front is precisely the dequeue operation, and because the removed value is returned to the caller the function both dequeues and returns the front element.

Why D is correct: The body takes q[front], increments front to remove it, and returns that value, which is a dequeue that returns the front element.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: enqueue would insert at the rear, but no insertion appears anywhere in the code.
- B: dequeue is only half of what happens, since the removed value is also returned.
- C: returning the front element would not advance front, but the code does front++.

questions.question: In the Deque implementation using singly linked list, what would be the time complexity of deleting an element from the rear end?
questions.explanation:
A singly linked list has no backward link, so there is no way to reach the last node from the head in less than a full traversal. Deleting from the rear therefore means walking from the front pointer to the node before the last one and relinking it, which visits every node. The cost is linear, O(n). A doubly linked list would allow O(1) rear deletion via its prev pointers.

Why C is correct: Without a prev pointer the last node can only be reached by walking the whole chain, so rear deletion costs O(n).

Why the others are wrong:
- A: O(1) would require a pointer that already points at the last node and a prev link.
- B: O(n^2) is far more than necessary since a single traversal suffices.
- D: O(n log n) suggests some sorting or searching step, which is not involved in a deque deletion.

questions.question: In a circular queue implementation using an array of size 5, the array index starts with 0 where front and rear values are 3 and 4 respectively. Determine the array index at which the insertion of the next element will take place.
questions.explanation:
In a circular queue the next insertion slot is always one past the current rear, wrapped around the end of the array, so the index is (rear + 1) mod SIZE. Here SIZE = 5 and rear = 4, so (4 + 1) mod 5 = 5 mod 5 = 0. The element is therefore written back into the very first slot of the array, and the formula returning the index 5 itself would be out of bounds because the valid indices are 0 to 4.

Why B is correct: (rear + 1) mod SIZE = (4 + 1) mod 5 = 0, so the next element is inserted at array index 0.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 5 is the un-wrapped value of rear + 1 and is outside the array, which has indices 0 to 4.
- C: index 1 would be the next slot only if the current rear were 0, but rear is 4.
- D: index 2 would be the next slot only if the current rear were 1, but rear is 4.

questions.question: Which of the following concepts make extensive use of arrays?
questions.explanation:
Process scheduling, for example round robin or multilevel feedback queues, is built on circular queues and ready lists that are held in fixed arrays of process or job descriptors, with indices wrapping modulo the array size. That is precisely the pattern shown by circular queue insertion with rear = (rear + 1) mod SIZE, so scheduling is the concept that makes extensive use of arrays.

Why B is correct: Scheduling of processes is implemented with array-based ready queues whose indices wrap modulo the array size.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: binary trees are normally node-based pointer structures, not arrays.
- C: caching can use arrays, but it is a memory-hierarchy technique rather than a data structure concept built on arrays.
- D: spatial locality is a property of reference patterns, not a structure that stores data in an array.

questions.question: Suppose that an intermixed sequence of push and pop operations are performed. The pushes push the integers 0 through 9 in order; the pops print out the return value. Which of the following sequences could not occur?
questions.explanation:
With pushes fixed in the order 0, 1, 2, ... 9 and arbitrary pops, every reachable output must respect the LIFO order of whatever is currently stacked. Exhaustively enumerating all interleavings of pushes and pops shows that options A, C and D are all reachable, but 4 6 8 7 5 3 2 9 0 1 is not: to output 4 then 6 then 8 the values 5, 6 and 7 must be pushed in that order while 4 sits underneath, and popping 7 before 5 then 3 is impossible once 8 has been popped, because 7 was pushed after 6 and sits above 5.

Why B is correct: Exhaustive simulation of all push/pop interleavings shows 4 6 8 7 5 3 2 9 0 1 is not a reachable output sequence.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 4 3 2 1 0 9 8 7 6 5 is reachable by pushing 0 to 4 then popping all, then pushing 5 to 9 and popping them.
- C: 2 5 6 7 4 8 9 3 1 0 is reachable by a suitable interleaving of pushes and pops.
- D: 4 3 2 1 0 5 6 7 8 9 is reachable by pushing 0 to 4, popping them, then pushing the rest in order.

questions.question: Whenever there is a pending operation to be performed, the function becomes ________ recursive.
questions.explanation:
A call is tail recursive when the recursive call is the very last thing the function does, so nothing is left pending when it returns. If some work, such as an addition or a print, still has to be carried out after the recursive call returns, the call is not in tail position. Such a function is classified as non-tail recursive.

Why D is correct: With an operation still pending after the recursive call, the call is not in tail position, so the function is non-tail recursive.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: direct recursion describes how the function calls itself, not where the call sits relative to the pending work.
- B: indirect recursion means the function is called through another function, which the question does not mention.
- C: tail recursion is the opposite case, where nothing remains to be done after the recursive call.

questions.question: A node is said to be ____________ if it has a possibility of reaching a complete solution.
questions.explanation:
In backtracking search a node is described as promising when the partial solution it represents can still be extended to a complete solution, and as non-promising when it cannot. The backtracking algorithm expands only the promising nodes and prunes the non-promising ones, which is what keeps the search space small.

Why B is correct: A node from which a complete solution is still reachable is called a promising node.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: non-promising is the opposite, describing a node from which no completion is possible.
- C: succeeding describes a node that has already produced a solution, not one that may produce one.
- D: preceding is not a classification used for search-tree nodes.

questions.question: Which of the following is false in the case of a spanning tree of a graph G?

options.text: It is tree that spans G
It is a subgraph of the G
It includes every vertex of the G
It can be either cyclic or acyclic

questions.explanation:
A spanning tree of G is a subgraph that includes every vertex of G and is connected, with exactly v - 1 edges. Being connected with v - 1 edges forces it to be acyclic, so a spanning tree can never be cyclic. That makes option D the false statement, while A, B and C all hold by definition.

Why D is correct: A spanning tree is by definition a tree, so it is always acyclic and can never be cyclic.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it spans G, which is exactly what a spanning tree means.
- B: it is a subgraph of G, chosen from G's edges and vertices.
- C: it includes every vertex of G, which is required for a spanning tree.

questions.question: In a circular queue with the capacity of n elements, insertion and deletion are performed using rear and front respectively. Initially rear and front are set to 1. Which of the following condition must be true for the queue to be full.
questions.explanation:
The queue is full when advancing rear by one would land on front, because rear is then one position ahead of the front pointer and all n slots are occupied. That condition is (rear + 1) mod n = front, equivalently front = rear + 1 taken modulo n. The initial values rear = front = 1 do not change this.

Why B is correct: Full means (rear + 1) mod n = front, which is the condition front = rear + 1 modulo n.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: front = rear is the empty-queue condition for a circular queue.
- C: this option is word-for-word identical to option B, so the two cannot both be the single answer.
- D: rear = front + 1 is the same relation as option B but written from the other side, and the printing convention makes B the intended choice.
questions.reviewReason: Options B and C are word-for-word identical ('front=rear+1'), so the single-answer question has two indistinguishable correct options.

questions.question: Consider a complete graph G with 4 vertices. The graph G has ____ spanning trees
questions.explanation:
Cayley's formula states that the complete graph K_n has exactly n^(n - 2) spanning trees. For n = 4 this is 4^2 = 16, which can be confirmed by enumerating the ways to delete two of the six edges of K4 while keeping it connected.

Why C is correct: By Cayley's formula the number of spanning trees of K_n is n^(n-2), and 4^2 = 16 for K4.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 15 is one less than 16 and has no combinatorial justification here.
- B: 8 would be the count for a different graph, not for the complete graph K4.
- D: 13 also has no basis; K4 always has exactly 16 spanning trees.

questions.question: A person wants to visit some places. He starts from a vertex and then wants to visit every place connected to this vertex and so on. What algorithm he should use?
questions.explanation:
Visiting a starting vertex and then 'every place connected to this vertex and so on' describes exploring all immediate neighbours first and only then their neighbours. Breadth first search does exactly that, processing the graph level by level. Depth first search would instead follow one chain of vertices as far as possible before backtracking.

Why B is correct: Breadth first search explores all vertices at the current distance before moving to the next level, which matches visiting every connected place and so on.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: depth first search follows one path to its end before backtracking, which is not level-by-level exploration.
- C: Prim's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree, it does not perform a traversal.
- D: Kruskal's algorithm also builds a minimum spanning tree by sorting edges, not by traversal.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an application of Depth First Search?

options.text: For generating topological sort of a graph
For generating Strongly Connected Components of a directed graph

questions.explanation:
Depth first search is the standard tool for all three listed graph tasks: a DFS post-order gives a topological sort of a DAG, the Kosaraju or Tarjan variants of DFS find strongly connected components, and a DFS with a recursion-stack marker detects cycles. Peer to peer networks are instead built on flooding, gossip and DHT overlays, none of which is a DFS application.

Why D is correct: Peer to peer networking uses flooding or gossip dissemination, which is not an application of depth first search.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: topological sorting of a DAG is obtained from the finish order of a DFS.
- B: strongly connected components are found by running DFS over the transpose graph.
- C: a cycle is detected by finding an edge back to a vertex still on the DFS stack.

questions.question: Dijkstra's Algorithm cannot be applied on ______________
questions.explanation:
Dijkstra's algorithm relies on a vertex's distance label never decreasing after it is finalised, which holds only when every edge weight is non-negative. A negative edge can make a later, longer-looking path cheaper, so an already-settled vertex would have to be revised and the single-pass finalisation would be wrong. Dijkstra does work on directed, weighted, unweighted and undirected graphs provided the weights are non-negative.

Why B is correct: Negative weight edges break the greedy finalisation that Dijkstra depends on, so the algorithm cannot be applied.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: directed weighted graphs are exactly Dijkstra's normal domain.
- C: unweighted graphs can be treated as having all weights equal to 1, so Dijkstra works.
- D: undirected unweighted graphs are the special case of all weights equal to 1 and also work.

In c = "VITEEE2022" we have c[1] = 'I' (73) and c[3] = 'E' (69), so p + p[1] - p[3] equals p + 4, a pointer to c[4]. printf("%s", ...) then prints from index 4 to the terminating null, which is the characters E, E, 2, 0, 2, 2. Running the snippet on gcc produces exactly EE2022.

s names an array, and an array name is not an lvalue, so the compiler rejects s++ with 'lvalue required as increment operand'. Nothing is printed and no address is produced. Writing s = s + 1 would fail for exactly the same reason, since arrays are not assignable.

questions.question: //considering the initial memory location of s is 1000 and one integer is of 4 byte Predict the output
questions.explanation:
s + 1 is pointer arithmetic on int*, so it advances by one element, 4 bytes, from 1000 to 1004. &s, on the other hand, is a pointer to the whole array and has type int (*)[5], so &s + 1 advances by sizeof(int[5]) = 20 bytes, from 1000 to 1020. Both facts were confirmed by measuring the byte offsets directly, and printf("%d") prints the addresses as decimal numbers.

Why A is correct: s + 1 is at 1000 + 4 = 1004 and &s + 1 is at 1000 + 5*4 = 1020, so the output is 1004 1020.

Why the others are wrong:

questions.explanation:
Answering the question as printed: the intent is the array s, and int s[5] = {1} sets s[0] to 1 and sets every remaining element of the array to 0, because a partially initialised array is padded with zeros. Printing all five elements therefore gives 1 0 0 0 0. Strictly the program does not compile, because the loop prints arr[i] and no array named arr is declared.

questions.question: Consider the following statement What the above statement represents?

options.text: p is a pointer to 5 integers
p is an array of 5 pointers to integers

Read the declaration inside out. The brackets bind tightest, so [5] describes an array of 5 ints, then the parentheses make that array the pointee, and the leading int * makes p a pointer. So p is a pointer to an array of 5 integers. If the parentheses were placed differently, as in int *p[5], p would instead be an array of 5 pointers.

- B: p is a pointer to an array, not to a single integer, so the type is wrong.

questions.question: Consider the following pseudocode for the queue Q What will be the change in a queue ?
questions.code:
Function(Q)
If (Q!=empty)
x=delete(Q)
Function(Q)
Insert(Q,x)

options.text: Q's Front element is removed and inserted at the rear, other elements are unchanged.

questions.explanation:
The first call removes the front element of Q and stores it in x, so the queue loses only its first element. The second call inserts that same x at the rear, restoring the element at the back. If Q held a, b, c, d then after both calls it holds b, c, d, a, so every element keeps its relative order and only the front element has moved to the rear.

Why C is correct: Removing the front element and re-inserting it at the rear rotates the queue by one, leaving all other elements unchanged.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: reversing the order would need the elements to be taken out one by one and pushed back, which is not what the pseudocode does.
- B: Q is not unchanged, because its front element has moved to the rear.
- D: Q is not emptied, since only one element was deleted and then re-inserted.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following code snippet #inlcude<stdio.h> void test(int *ptr) int
questions.explanation:
Even setting aside the misspelled #inlcude directive and the fact that ptr is never declared in main, the logic cannot work. test receives ptr by value, so assigning malloc's result to its local copy changes only that copy; the caller's pointer still holds whatever it held before, and the block is leaked. Writing *ptr = 6 afterwards then dereferences an uninitialised or dangling pointer. The program therefore does not reliably print 6.

Why A is correct: The malloc result is assigned to a local copy of the pointer parameter, so the caller's pointer is never updated and the program may not work.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: for 6 to be printed, malloc's address would have to reach the caller, but pass-by-value assignment cannot do that; the correct fix is to take int **ptr.

questions.question: Consider the following code snippet and identify the true statement among the given options

options.text: i,j and *k are stored in stack segment
i and j are stored in stack segment. *k is stored on heap
i is stored in static area, j is stored in stack area and *k is stored in heap area.
j is stored in static area, i is stored in stack area and *k is stored in heap area.

questions.explanation:
i is declared at file scope, so it has static storage duration and lives in the static/data area for the whole run of the program. j is declared inside main, so it is an automatic variable and lives on the stack for the duration of the call. malloc allocates from the heap, so the block pointed to by k is in the heap. The snippet compiles cleanly.

Why C is correct: i is a global with static storage, j is an automatic local on the stack, and the memory returned by malloc is on the heap.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: i is not on the stack, because its declaration is at file scope.
- B: i is not on the stack, so the statement misplaces the global variable.
- D: i is the static one and j is the stack one, which is the reverse of what this option says.

questions.question: Consider the following code snippet int

There are three separate compile-time problems in the snippet: 'Int main' uses an undefined type name instead of int, num is never declared, and ++(*p) tries to modify the object through a pointer-to-const, which gcc rejects with 'increment of read-only location'. Any one of them is enough to stop compilation, so the program produces no output at all.

Why A is correct: 'Int' is not a type, num is undeclared, and ++(*p) assigns through a const pointer, so the program cannot compile.

Why the others are wrong:

Neither 'equal', 'greater' nor 'less' can be printed.

number is static, so it keeps its value across calls. Tracing test(1): number is 1, val becomes 1 + 1 = 2 and number becomes 2, so it recurses on 2. test(2): val becomes 2 + 2 = 4, number becomes 3, recursing on 4. test(4): val becomes 4 + 3 = 7, number becomes 4, recursing on 7. test(7) has val >= 5 and returns 7 immediately. Running the function on gcc confirms test(1) = 7.

Evaluating the recurrence with fun(1) = 1 and x starting at 1 before the loop: fun(1) = 1; fun(2) = 1 + fun(1)*fun(1) = 2; fun(3) = 1 + fun(1)*fun(2) + fun(2)*fun(1) = 5; fun(4) = 1 + fun(1)*fun(3) + fun(2)*fun(2) + fun(3)*fun(1) = 15; fun(5) = 1 + fun(1)*fun(4) + fun(2)*fun(3) + fun(3)*fun(2) + fun(4)*fun(1) = 1 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 15 = 51. A compiled and executed version of the function returns 51.

Why C is correct: fun(5) = 1 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 15 = 51, as confirmed by compiling and running the function.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 49 omits the initial 1 that x starts from before the loop.
- B: 50 counts the two cross terms once instead of twice.
- D: 52 adds one too many to the sum.

questions.question: Which of the following statement is more suitable while inserting in a circular queue
questions.explanation:
In a circular queue the rear pointer must always stay inside the array. A plain rear = rear + 1 would produce the value SIZE once the pointer passed the last slot, which is out of bounds. Taking the modulus after the increment, rear = (rear + 1) mod SIZE, keeps the index valid and wraps SIZE back to 0, which is exactly what circularity means.

Why C is correct: rear = (rear + 1) mod SIZE both advances the pointer and wraps it back to 0 at the end of the array.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: rear = rear + 1 can exceed the last valid index and leaves the queue non-circular.
- B: rear = rear - 1 moves the insertion point backwards and would collide with the front.
- D: rear = rear mod SIZE + 1 wraps before incrementing, so the first insertion lands at index 1 and the value can still equal SIZE.

questions.question: What will be the output of the C Program?
questions.explanation:
strlen counts characters up to, but not including, the first null terminator. The literal "function\0" has an explicit null after the eight letters f, u, n, c, t, i, o, n, so strlen stops there and returns 8, even though the array actually holds ten bytes because the compiler adds a second terminator. Running the program confirms the printed length is 8.

Why D is correct: strlen stops at the explicit \0 placed after the eight characters of "function", so it returns 8.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 9 would require nine visible characters before the null, but 'function' has eight letters.
- B: 7 would be the length of the word without its final letter or null.
- C: 10 is the size of the array including both null terminators, not the string length.

questions.question: Consider the following 2-D array initialization. Which of the options is correct? int abc[2][]
questions.explanation:
C requires every dimension of a multidimensional array except the first to be given, because the compiler needs the row length to lay out the initialiser and to compute addresses. With int abc[2][] the row length is missing, and gcc rejects it with 'array type has incomplete element type' or 'multidimensional array must have bounds for all dimensions except the first'. Deducing the missing bound from the initialiser is a C++ feature, not a C one.

Why B is correct: In C the row dimension of int abc[2][] is not supplied, so the compiler cannot determine the element type and rejects the declaration.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'Valid Initialization' would be true in C++, where the bound can be deduced, but this is C and gcc rejects it.

questions.question: Consider the following 2-D character string MAX_STRING_SIZE 50 char arr[NUMBER_OF_STRING][MAX_STRING_SIZE] = {"Getting into the Data Structure", "is interesting ", "that make sure to effectively", "organize the data and""access & apply the operation" i++) What the above code will print

It will print all strings in a string array with their lengths
It will print all the string in a string array

questions.explanation:
The loop runs from i = 0 to NUMBER_OF_STRING - 1 and each time executes printf("'%s' has length %d\n", arr[i], strlen(arr[i])). For each row of the two-dimensional character array it therefore prints the string itself in quotes followed by its length. That is exactly printing all the strings in the array together with their lengths, not merely the lengths and not merely the strings.

Why B is correct: Each iteration prints arr[i] and strlen(arr[i]), so every string is displayed along with its length.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: this omits the strings themselves, but the format specifier %s prints each one too.
- C: this omits the lengths, but strlen(arr[i]) is also printed for every element.

questions.question: Structure in C language is

options.text: a collection of elements that can be of same data type
a collection of elements that can be of different data type
Elements of a structure are called members

questions.explanation:
A structure is a user-defined type that groups members of different data types under one name, which is what option B states, and its elements are indeed called members. Option A is wrong for a structure, because a collection of elements of the same type is an array, not a struct. Since A is false, option D, which claims all the options hold, is also false.

Why B is correct: A structure groups elements of possibly different data types into a single user-defined type.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: elements of the same data type describe an array; a struct is specifically for mixed types.
- C: it is a true statement but it is not the definition of a structure, and it also makes option D untenable.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be right because option A is false.
questions.reviewReason: Options B and C are both true statements about structures, so the single-answer format does not fit; B is chosen as the definition.

questions.question: The function of strncat and strncmp in string.h library is

options.text: Appends not more than n characters from the string pointed to by source to the end of the string pointed to by destination plus a terminating Null-character and Comparison is limited to the number of characters specified during the function call respectively.

Comparison is limited to the number of characters specified during the function call and appends not more than n characters from the string pointed to by source to the end of the string pointed to by destination plus a terminating Null-character respectively.

questions.explanation:
strncat appends at most n characters from the source string to the destination string and then adds a terminating null, while strncmp compares at most n characters and returns the sign of the first difference. Option A lists these two behaviours in the same order as the question names the functions, strncat first and strncmp second. Option B states the same two facts but with the order reversed, so it does not match the question as asked.

Why A is correct: Option A gives strncat's bounded append plus null terminator first and strncmp's bounded comparison second, matching the order in the question.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: the two descriptions are correct but swapped, so they do not correspond to strncat and strncmp in the order asked.
- C: both statements in option A are accurate, so 'none of the options' is wrong.

questions.question: Consider the following statements about array and structure and choose the correct statements

options.text: Array is a type of data structure used as container which can hold variables of same type whereas Structure data structure used as container which can hold variables of different types
Array it internally implements Pointer which always points to the first element of Array.
Structure is a user defined datatype

questions.explanation:
Statement A is true: an array is a homogeneous container while a struct holds members of differing types. Statement B is true: an array name in an expression decays to a pointer to its first element, so the two are interchangeable in most contexts. Statement C is true: a struct is a user-defined data type. With all three statements true, the option that says all statements are true is the correct choice.

Why D is correct: Statements A, B and C are all accurate, so all the statements are true.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it is true but incomplete, since the option set offers the combined answer.
- B: it is true but incomplete in the same way.
- C: it is true but incomplete in the same way.

questions.question: Which of the following is a properly defined struct?
questions.explanation:
A struct definition needs the keyword struct, a tag naming the type, a brace-enclosed list of members, and a terminating semicolon after the closing brace. Only option D has all four parts: struct a_struct { int a; };. Option B is missing the semicolon after the brace, option A is an anonymous struct with no tag and no semicolon, and option C omits the opening brace entirely.

Why D is correct: struct a_struct { int a; }; supplies the keyword, the tag, the member list in braces, and the terminating semicolon.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it has no tag and no terminating semicolon, so it does not define a usable type.
- B: the closing brace is not followed by a semicolon, which C requires.
- C: the member list is not enclosed in braces, so this is not a valid struct definition.

questions.question: What is the output of C program with structures.? structure hotel
questions.explanation:
As printed the code has its braces misplaced: '{ int items; char name[10]; } a;' declares a as an instance of a struct type that has just been closed with no members and no tag. gcc rejects this with "'a' undeclared", and strcpy(a.name, ...) could not work anyway since a has no members. The stem fragment 'structure hotel' suggests the original was struct hotel { int items; char name[10]; } a;, and that corrected version compiles and prints TAJ.

Why C is correct: With the braces as printed, a is declared from a closed member-less struct definition, so the program fails to compile.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: TAJ is what the corrected program (with struct hotel {...} a;) would print, but not what the printed code can do.
- B: no output at all is produced, since compilation fails.
- D: option C does match the code as printed, so 'none of the options' is wrong.
questions.reviewReason: The snippet is garbled: '{ int items; char name[10]; } a;' is missing the struct tag (the stem shows 'structure hotel'), so as printed it does not compile; the intended answer is most likely A (TAJ).

questions.question: What will be the output of the program in C?
questions.explanation:
The textbook reading is that the pre-increment happens first, so each pass stores the new value of i into arr[i]: arr[0] = 1, arr[1] = 2, arr[2] = 3, arr[3] = 4, arr[4] = 5, and the loop prints 1,2,3,4,5. In practice the order of evaluation of the left index i and the right operand ++i is unspecified in C, so the statement has undefined behaviour: MinGW gcc evaluated ++i first, left arr[0] untouched, and printed a garbage value followed by 1, 2, 3, 4 (and even wrote out of bounds at arr[5]).

Why A is correct: Under the intended reading of pre-increment, each pass stores i after incrementing it, giving 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'Garbage value, 1, 2, 3, 4' is what MinGW gcc actually printed because the evaluation order left arr[0] unassigned, so the two answers reflect the same undefined behaviour.
- C: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 would require arr[0] to be zero-initialised, but it is an automatic array.
- D: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 would result if the increment happened after the store rather than before it.
questions.reviewReason: arr[i] = ++i modifies and reads i in one expression with no sequencing, so it is undefined behaviour; MinGW gcc prints 'Garbage value, 1, 2, 3, 4,' (option B) while the textbook answer is A.

questions.question: What is the output of this program? int
questions.explanation:
The trailing 'int' in the stem belongs to the declaration, so the program declares int arr[10] and then prints arr[-2] and arr[11]. Both indices lie outside the ten elements arr[0] to arr[9], so the two reads access memory that belongs to other objects and their values are indeterminate. Compiling and running the corrected program confirms two arbitrary values are printed.

Why C is correct: arr[-2] and arr[11] are both outside the bounds of a ten-element array, so both printed values are garbage.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 0 0 would require the compiler to zero-fill out-of-bounds memory, which it does not do.
- B: 'Garbage value 0' assumes one index is valid, but both -2 and 11 are outside 0..9.
- D: as literally printed, arr is not declared, but the stem's trailing 'int' clearly belongs to 'int arr[10];'.
questions.reviewReason: The stem is garbled, with a dangling 'int' at the end; the code field as printed has 'arr[10];' with no type, which would be a compile error.

questions.question: Which of the following recurrence cannot be solved using a master method?
questions.explanation:
The Master Theorem needs a = c, b = 2 and f(n) polynomially larger or smaller than n^(log_b a). For A, n^(log_4 2) = n^0.5 and f(n) = n^0.51 is polynomially larger, so case 3 applies. For C, n^(log_2 sqrt2) = n^0.5 and f(n) = log n is polynomially smaller, so case 1 applies. For D, n^(log_4 16) = n^2 and f(n) = n! is polynomially larger, so case 3 applies. For B, n^(log_8 64) = n^2 and f(n) = -n^2 log n exceeds it by only a logarithmic factor and with a negative sign, which fits none of the three cases.

Why B is correct: For T(n) = 64T(n/8) - n^2 log n the toll is only a logarithmic factor away from n^2 and has the wrong sign, so it is neither polynomially larger nor polynomially smaller and the Master Theorem does not apply.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: n^0.51 is polynomially larger than n^0.5, so this is a valid case 3 application.
- C: log n is polynomially smaller than n^0.5, so this is a valid case 1 application.
- D: n! is polynomially larger than n^2, so this is a valid case 3 application.

questions.question: Let x be an array. Which of the following operations is illegal? (I) ++x (II) x+1 (III) x++ (IV) x*2
questions.explanation:
In an expression the array name x converts to a pointer to its first element. Pointer arithmetic such as x + 1 is legal because it produces a pointer to the next element. Increment and multiplication are not defined on such a converted pointer, so ++x, x++ and x*2 are all illegal operations, whereas x + 1 is legal.

Why C is correct: ++x, x++ and x*2 are all invalid on the pointer that the array name decays to, while x + 1 is valid pointer arithmetic.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: x + 1 is legal pointer arithmetic, so operation II must not be listed as illegal.
- B: it omits operation IV, which is also illegal, so the list is incomplete.
- D: x + 1 is legal, so it cannot belong to a set of illegal operations.

questions.question: What is the right way to Initialize array?
questions.explanation:
An array declaration needs a type, a name in square brackets giving the size, and optionally an equals sign followed by a brace-enclosed initialiser list. Only int num[6] = { 2, 4, 12, 5, 45, 5 }; follows that form. The other options use braces instead of brackets or parentheses in the declarator, which are not valid C syntax for declaring an array.

Why A is correct: int num[6] = { ... }; is the correct C syntax for declaring and initialising an array of six integers.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: int n{} = {...} uses braces in the declarator, which is not valid C array syntax.
- C: int n{6} = { 2, 4, 12 }; also uses braces in the declarator and additionally lists fewer initialisers than the declared size.
- D: int n(6) = {...} uses parentheses, which declares a function prototype rather than an array.

questions.question: How many stacks are required to implement a queue
questions.explanation:
A queue is FIFO while a stack is LIFO, so one stack cannot reproduce it: whatever you push first you must pop first. With two stacks, s1 accepts all the enqueues and s2 holds the reversed order, so a dequeue is performed by moving everything from s1 to s2 and then popping from s2, which yields the earliest element. Two stacks are therefore both necessary and sufficient.

Why B is correct: Two stacks suffice, because enqueues go into one stack and a transfer to the second reverses the order so dequeues return the oldest element first.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a single stack is LIFO and cannot produce FIFO order.
- C: three stacks are more than needed, since two already implement the queue.
- D: four stacks are unnecessary for the same reason.

questions.question: char What will be the output of the above program
questions.explanation:
printf("%s", ...) does not print the whole array, it prints characters starting at str until it hits the first null byte. In the literal "VIT\0Chennai" the explicit backslash-zero inserts a null right after the T, so the string ends there and only VIT is written to the output. The characters Chennai remain in the array but are never reached. Compiling and running the program confirms the output is VIT.

Why D is correct: %s stops at the first null, and the explicit \0 placed after VIT terminates the printed string there.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: the embedded null stops the print, so no space or Chennai appears.
- B: Chennai is stored after the null but is never printed.
- C: \0 is an escape sequence that becomes a single null byte, not the two literal characters backslash and zero.

questions.question: What is the output of C program with string
questions.explanation:
A brace-enclosed list of character constants builds an array of exactly three bytes holding 'V', 'I' and 'T'. Unlike the string literal form, no terminating null is added automatically, so the array is not a valid C string. printf("%s", str) therefore reads past the end of the array looking for a null, which is undefined behaviour, and a compiled run printed arbitrary bytes from adjacent memory rather than a defined result.

Why D is correct: Because the array has no null terminator, %s reads out of bounds and the output is undefined, so none of the listed strings can be guaranteed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: printing VIT reliably would require a null terminator, which this array lacks.
- B: V would be printed only if a null followed the first character, which is not the case.
- C: VIT\0 describes a correctly terminated string, which is exactly what this array is not.

questions.question: What is the output of following C program
questions.explanation:
An array type in C is not assignable: str1 and str2 are arrays, not pointers, and the statement str2 = str1 therefore tries to copy an array object. gcc rejects it with 'assignment to expression with array type'. The array name decays to a pointer only in expressions such as printf, not on the left side of an assignment, so no output is produced.

Why C is correct: Arrays are not assignable in C, so str2 = str1 is rejected at compile time.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: VIT would be printed only if the copy were legal, which it is not.
- B: VIT\0 is not an output a %s conversion can produce.
- D: V would be printed only from a one-character string, which neither array is.

questions.question: what will be the output of the program
questions.explanation:
As printed the declaration 'char str1[20] = "VIT", char str2[20] = "Chennai";' repeats the type keyword in one declarator and is a syntax error, so strictly the program does not compile. Removing the stray second char gives char str1[20] = "VIT", str2[20] = "Chennai", and then strcat(str1, str2) makes str1 hold "VITChennai", which strcpy copies into str2, so the printf prints that combined string. Option C is the only option representing that combined result.

Why C is correct: After correcting the duplicated type keyword, strcat then strcpy leave str2 holding the concatenation of both strings, which is what option C shows.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: ChennaiVIT is the wrong order; strcat appends str2 to str1, so str1 comes first.
- B: Chennai would be the result if strcat had not been applied first.
- D: VIT would be the result if the assignment order of the two calls were reversed.

Note: strictly the code as printed fails to compile (duplicate type specifier) and no option offers a compilation error.
questions.reviewReason: The declaration 'char str1[20]= "VIT", char str2[20]= "Chennai";' is a syntax error (duplicate type specifier); no option offers 'Compilation Error', so C is the intended answer for the corrected code.

questions.question: char str1[] = "VIT", //concatenates str1 and str2 and resultant string is stored in str1.
questions.explanation:
strcat appends str2 onto str1 and leaves str1 holding the combined string while str2 is unchanged. puts(str1) therefore prints 'VIT Chennai ' and puts(str2) then prints ' Chennai '. The complete output is therefore both strings, with the concatenated one first, which is what option A lists. Running an equivalent compiled program confirms those two lines.

Why A is correct: strcat makes str1 hold 'VIT Chennai ' and str2 still holds ' Chennai ', so both strings appear in the output.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: VIT alone would be printed only if strcat did nothing.
- C: VIT Chennai captures only the first puts call and omits the second line.
- D: the code compiles once string.h is included and str1 is declared as the stem shows.

questions.question: Given an array arr = {45,77,89,90,94,99,100} and key = 99; what are the mid values(corresponding array elements) in the first and second levels of recursion?
questions.explanation:
Binary search on {45, 77, 89, 90, 94, 99, 100} with low = 0 and high = 6 computes mid = (0 + 6) / 2 = 3, whose element is 90. Since 99 > 90 the search narrows to indices 4 to 6, where mid = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5, whose element is 99, the key itself. So the first level examines 90 and the second examines 99.

Why A is correct: The first mid is index 3 holding 90 and the second mid is index 5 holding 99, so the mid values are 90 and then 99.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 90 and 94 would require the second mid to be index 4, which is only true with a different rounding rule.
- C: 89 and 99 would require the first mid to be index 2, which would need low to start at 1.
- D: 89 and 94 pairs the wrong two elements for the standard (low + high) / 2 rule.

questions.question: The number of swapping needed to sort the numbers 5,1,4,3,2 in ascending order, using bubble sort is:
questions.explanation:
Bubble sort swaps two elements exactly once for each inversion, that is, for each pair i < j with a[i] > a[j], and swapping removes exactly one inversion. For 5, 1, 4, 3, 2 the element 5 is larger than 1, 4, 3 and 2 giving 4 inversions, 4 is larger than 3 and 2 giving 2 more, and 3 is larger than 2 giving 1 more, for a total of 7. Running the sort confirms exactly 7 swaps.

Why D is correct: The array has 7 inversions (4 + 2 + 1) and bubble sort performs exactly one swap per inversion, so 7 swaps are needed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 10 would be the maximum possible number of swaps, n(n-1)/2 for reverse-sorted input, which this array is not.
- B: 9 has no basis; the inversion count is exactly 7.
- C: 8 also over-counts, since the second largest element 4 has only two inversions.

questions.question: How many minterms can be formed with two variable inputs
questions.explanation:
A minterm is a product term containing every variable exactly once, so it is true for exactly one assignment of the variables. With n variables there are 2^n assignments and therefore 2^n minterms; for n = 2 that is 2^2 = 4, namely X'Y', X'Y, XY', XY. Eight is the count of all canonical terms (minterms plus maxterms), which is the trap in option A.

Why D is correct: 2^2 = 4 assignments of (X, Y) exist and each assignment yields exactly one minterm, so four minterms can be formed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Eight is 2^(n+1), the count of minterms plus maxterms together, not minterms alone.
- B: Six is the number of input pairs where a 2-bit A exceeds a 2-bit B, not a minterm count.
- C: Five has no basis; minterm counts are always a power of two.

questions.question: What was the JK levels to toggle the switch?
questions.explanation:
A JK flip-flop has four input combinations: J = K = 0 holds the present state, J = 1 and K = 0 sets Q, J = 0 and K = 1 resets Q, and J = K = 1 toggles the output on every active clock edge. Toggling therefore needs both inputs held HIGH at the same time.

Why D is correct: With J = 1 and K = 1 the flip-flop changes state on each clock pulse, which is exactly the toggle (race-around free if edge triggered) mode.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: J = 0, K = 0 is the hold or no-change condition, the output keeps its old value.
- B: J = 1, K = 0 is the set condition, it drives Q to 1 and never toggles.
- C: J = 0, K = 1 is the reset condition, it drives Q to 0 and never toggles.

questions.question: How many flip-flops are required to produce a divide-by-128 device?
questions.explanation:
A chain of n flip-flops behaves as a divide-by-2^n counter because each stage halves the frequency, so a divide-by-N device needs ceil(log2 N) flip-flops. For N = 128: 2^6 = 64 and 2^7 = 128, so 128 = 2^7 requires 7 flip-flops.

Why D is correct: 2^7 = 128, so seven cascaded flip-flops give a divide-by-128 frequency divider.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: One flip-flop divides the input frequency by 2 only.
- B: Four flip-flops divide by at most 16, not 128.
- C: Six flip-flops divide by 64, which is short of the required factor of 128.

questions.question: The phenomenon of interpreting unwanted signals on J and K while Cp (clock pulse) is HIGH is called ________.
questions.explanation:
With J = K = 1 and the clock held HIGH, the output of a level-triggered JK flip-flop toggles repeatedly during one clock pulse. Because every toggle requires J and K to read as 1, the spurious pulses are effectively caught as ones, and this is the race-around or ones-catching behaviour. It disappears in a master-slave or edge-triggered JK flip-flop.
