- B: Three values ignores either the 11 or the 12 outcome.
- D: Eight is impossible, there are only six interleavings in total.

questions.question: The program follows to use a shared binary semaphore T. Process A Process B B1: T is set to 0 before either process begins execution and, as before, X is set to 5. Now, how many different values of X are possible after both processes finish executing?
questions.explanation:
Process B cannot execute wait(T) until A has executed signal(T), and A issues that signal only after both A1 and A2 have finished. So A1 and A2 always complete first, giving X = 5 times 2 = 10, and only then does B run, setting Z = 10 plus 1 = 11 and X = 11. Every legal execution therefore ends with the same value of X.

Why A is correct: The semaphore forces A to finish both statements before B runs, so X is always 11.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Two values would require the interleaving freedom that the semaphore removes.
- C: Three values cannot occur, the order is fixed by the semaphore.
- D: Four values is the answer to the unsynchronised version, not this one.

questions.question: Transient operating system code is a code that ____________
questions.explanation:
Some operating system code is resident, permanently present in memory, such as the kernel and the scheduler. Transient code, by contrast, is loaded into memory only when it is needed, for example a device driver or a system call routine, and is removed again afterwards. That is why it comes and goes as required.

Why C is correct: Transient code is loaded into memory on demand and removed when no longer needed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Always staying in memory describes resident code.
- B: Never entering memory describes code that is never loaded, which is not transient code.
- D: Accessibility is not the defining property.

questions.question: All processes share a semaphore variable mutex, initialized to 1. Each process must execute wait(mutex) before entering the critical section and signal(mutex) afterward. Suppose a process executes in the following manner. ..... critical section ..... In this situation :
questions.code:
signal(mutex);
wait(mutex);

options.text: processes will starve to enter critical section
several processes maybe executing in their critical section

questions.explanation:
Because the process signals the mutex before it waits on it, and never signals it again after leaving the critical section, the net effect is that the semaphore value is only driven downwards. Each iteration consumes one unit that nobody returns, so after a few iterations the value reaches zero with every process still wanting to enter. All of them then block forever, which is a deadlock.

Why A is correct: Net signal and wait equal zero over an iteration and nothing ever releases the mutex afterwards, so everyone blocks.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Starvation would need the mutex to keep being released to somebody.
- C: Several processes in the critical section can occur briefly, but the deadlock option is the decisive outcome.
- D: Incorrect, the situation ends in deadlock.

questions.question: All processes share a semaphore variable mutex, initialized to 1. Each process must execute wait(mutex) before entering the critical section and signal(mutex) afterward. Suppose a process executes in the following manner. ..... critical section .....
questions.code:
wait(mutex);
wait(mutex);

options.text: processes will starve to enter critical section
several processes maybe executing in their critical section

questions.explanation:
The process waits on the binary mutex twice in a row. Since the mutex starts at 1, the first wait consumes it and the second wait finds the value already 0, so the process blocks and can never be released, because nothing will signal it. A process blocking itself in this way is the simplest textbook deadlock.

Why A is correct: The second wait on an already zero mutex blocks the process for ever.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Starvation needs other processes to keep taking the mutex, which is not the issue here.
- C: Mutual exclusion still holds, so several processes cannot be in the critical section.
- D: Incorrect, only the deadlock option describes the outcome.

questions.question: Consider the methods used by processes P1 and P2 for accessing their critical sections whenever needed, as given below. The initial values of shared boolean variables S1 and S2 are randomly assigned. Method used by P1 : Critical section Method used by P2 : Critical section S2 = Which of the following statements describes properties achieved?
questions.explanation:
P1 is allowed in only when S1 differs from S2, and P2 is allowed in only when S1 equals S2, so the two tests are complementary and at most one process can ever be inside the critical section. Progress is not guaranteed: if S1 is 1 and S2 is 0 and P1 does not want to enter while P2 does, P2 must wait until P1 runs and executes S1 = S2, which may never happen. Strict alternation therefore blocks progress.

Why A is correct: The complementary flag tests give mutual exclusion but enforce strict alternation, which breaks progress.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Mutual exclusion does hold, so this pair is impossible.
- C: Mutual exclusion does hold.
- D: Progress does not hold.

questions.question: What is a reusable resource?

options.text: that can be used by one process at a time and is not depleted by that use
that can be used by more than one process at a time
that can be shared between various threads

questions.explanation:
Resources are classified as reusable or consumable. A reusable resource, such as a printer, a CPU or a memory area, can be used again after a process releases it, so use by one process does not deplete it, though it must be used by only one process at a time. A consumable resource, such as printer paper, is used up as it is used.

Why A is correct: A reusable resource can be reused after release and is not depleted by that use.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Being usable by many processes at once describes a sharable resource, not a reusable one.
- C: Sharing between threads is about access, not about depletion.
- D: Incorrect, a precise definition exists.

questions.question: A system is in the safe state if ____________

options.text: the system can allocate resources to each process in some order and still avoid a deadlock

questions.explanation:
The system is in a safe state if the resources can be allocated to the processes one at a time so that each of them can finish and release its resources, leaving the remaining processes satisfiable. Saying that there exists such a safe sequence and saying that resources can be allocated in some order to avoid deadlock are two wordings of exactly this one condition. Since both statements are true, the option that covers both is the right key.

Why C is correct: Both statements A and B express the single definition of a safe state, so all of them applies.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: True, but it is only one of the two equivalent wordings.
- B: True, but it is only one of the two equivalent wordings.
- D: Incorrect, the condition is well defined.
questions.reviewReason: Options A and B are both correct restatements of the same definition, so the question has two defensible keys; C (all) is used to cover both, but a reviewer may prefer A or B alone.

questions.question: The circular wait condition can be prevented by ____________

options.text: defining a linear ordering of resource types

questions.explanation:
Circular wait arises when the resources are ordered differently by each process, so that a chain of holdings forms a loop. Declaring a total order of all resource types and requiring that a process may request only resources with a higher order than the ones it holds makes such a loop impossible to form.

Why A is correct: Imposing a linear ordering of resource types breaks the cycle of waiting.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Using threads has no bearing on the circular wait condition.
- C: Pipes are an IPC mechanism, not a prevention technique.
- D: Incorrect, only the ordering technique prevents circular wait.

questions.question: A problem encountered in multitasking when a process is perpetually denied necessary resources is called ____________
questions.explanation:
Starvation is the situation in which a process is ready to run but is continually denied the CPU or the resources it needs, so it waits indefinitely while the system as a whole keeps making progress. A deadlock, in contrast, involves a set of processes that are all waiting for each other, so no progress is possible at all.

Why B is correct: Perpetual denial of necessary resources to a single process is starvation.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Deadlock needs a cycle of mutual waiting, not just denial to one process.
- C: Inversion is a priority inversion performance problem.
- D: Aging is the cure for starvation, not its name.

questions.question: To avoid deadlock ____________

options.text: there must be a fixed number of resources to allocate
resource allocation must be done only once
all deadlocked processes must be aborted

questions.explanation:
One standard deadlock prevention technique negates the hold-and-wait condition by requiring a process to request all the resources it will ever need in a single request, and to be granted them all at once. That is the meaning of doing the resource allocation only once; the process then either gets everything or waits without holding anything. Aborting deadlocked processes is a recovery technique, not avoidance, and resource inversion is unrelated to deadlock.

Why B is correct: A single all-or-nothing allocation request removes the hold-and-wait condition and thus prevents deadlock.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: A fixed number of resources is not in itself a deadlock prevention rule.
- C: Aborting processes is recovery after deadlock, not avoidance.
- D: Inversion technique refers to priority inversion, not deadlock.
questions.reviewReason: The widely circulated answer key for this item gives (a), but a fixed number of resources is not a recognised deadlock avoidance technique, while (b) is the standard all-or-nothing request; the option set is poorly worded.

questions.question: The request and release of resources are ___________
questions.explanation:
User processes cannot touch resource tables or device registers directly. They obtain and release resources by making system calls, such as request and release, which the kernel validates and executes in kernel mode. Those calls, not user commands or interrupts, are the interface through which resources are requested and given back.

Why C is correct: Requesting and releasing resources are done through system calls.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: They are not command line statements issued from the shell.
- B: Interrupts are device-generated signals, not the user's way of asking for resources.
- D: They are not separate special programs.

questions.question: What are Multithreaded programs?

options.text: not at all prone to deadlocks

questions.explanation:
Threads of the same process share the address space, the open files and the process resources, so they compete for the same mutexes and can lock each other out. Since each thread may hold several of these shared locks at once, the number of possible circular waits grows and multithreaded programs are more prone to deadlock than single-threaded ones. They are certainly not free of deadlock.

Why B is correct: Shared resources held by several threads create more circular waits, so multithreaded programs are more prone to deadlock.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Sharing makes deadlock more likely, not less.
- C: Deadlock is fully possible in a multithreaded program.
- D: Incorrect, a definite relation exists.

questions.question: The portion of the process scheduler in an operating system that dispatches processes is concerned with ____________

options.text: assigning ready processes to waiting queue
assigning running processes to blocked queue

questions.explanation:
The dispatching part of the scheduler takes a process that is sitting in the ready queue and makes it the running process, which means assigning a ready process to the CPU. Moves into the waiting or blocked queue belong to the state-transition code, not to the dispatcher.

Why C is correct: The dispatcher assigns a ready process to the CPU.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Ready processes are not assigned to the waiting queue by the dispatcher.
- B: A running process becomes blocked only when it waits for an event.
- D: Incorrect, only the ready to running transfer is described.
questions.reviewReason: Near-duplicate stem of q_0300 (extractionFlags duplicate-stem-of), with the option letters permuted; answered independently as instructed.

questions.question: For Mutual exclusion to prevail in the system ____________

options.text: at least one resource must be held in a non sharable mode
the processor must be a uniprocessor rather than a multiprocessor
there must be at least one resource in a sharable mode

questions.explanation:
Mutual exclusion can only exist where a resource is not sharable. A sharable resource, such as a read-only file or a buffer that is written by only one process at a time by convention, imposes no hardware or software exclusion, so for mutual exclusion to prevail at least one resource must be held in a non-sharable mode with exclusion enforced.

Why A is correct: Mutual exclusion requires at least one resource to be held in a non-sharable mode.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Multiprocessors still need mutual exclusion, the processor count is irrelevant.
- C: A sharable resource provides no exclusion at all.
- D: Incorrect, only one statement holds.

questions.question: For a Hold and wait condition to prevail ____________

options.text: A process must be not be holding a resource, but waiting for one to be freed, and then request to acquire it
A process must be holding at least one resource and waiting to acquire additional resources that are being held by other processes
A process must hold at least one resource and not be waiting to acquire additional resources

questions.explanation:
Hold and wait is the second of the four necessary conditions for deadlock. It means that a process keeps at least one resource that it already holds while it waits for additional resources that other processes are holding. If a process never held anything while waiting, the condition would not hold.

Why B is correct: The process holds some resources while waiting for others held by other processes.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Not holding anything while waiting is precisely the negation of the condition.
- C: Holding without waiting is not hold and wait.
- D: Incorrect, a precise definition exists.

questions.question: Deadlock prevention is a set of methods ___________

options.text: to ensure that at least one of the necessary conditions cannot hold
to ensure that all of the necessary conditions do not hold
to decide if the requested resources for a process have to be given or not

questions.explanation:
Deadlock is possible only when all four necessary conditions, mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait, hold at the same time. A prevention scheme therefore only has to destroy one of them, not all four, which is what option A says.

Why A is correct: Prevention ensures that at least one of the four necessary conditions cannot hold.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Destroying all four conditions is far stronger than necessary.
- C: Deciding whether to grant a request is deadlock avoidance, not prevention.
- D: Recovering from a deadlock happens after it occurs.

questions.question: For sharable resources, mutual exclusion ____________

options.text: may be or may not be required

questions.explanation:
The mutual exclusion condition applies only to resources that are not sharable. If a resource may be used by several processes at the same time, for example a read-only file, there is nothing to exclude and no mutual exclusion is required for it.

Why B is correct: A sharable resource needs no mutual exclusion.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Requiring exclusion contradicts the definition of a sharable resource.
- C: The requirement is well defined, it simply does not apply here.
- D: Incorrect, a clear statement exists.

questions.question: The disadvantage of a process being allocated all its resources before beginning its execution is ____________
questions.explanation:
The all-or-nothing allocation rule avoids deadlock by making a process wait until everything it needs is free, but that wait is pure waste: the resources sit idle while the process waits, and long processes can hold large holdings for a long time. Resources are therefore poorly utilised, and processes may starve waiting for a complete bundle.

Why B is correct: Waiting for an entire resource bundle leaves resources idle, so utilisation is low.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Low CPU utilisation is not the characteristic drawback of this scheme.
- C: High resource utilisation is the opposite of the truth.
- D: Incorrect, a real drawback exists.

questions.question: To ensure no preemption, if a process is holding some resources and requests another resource that cannot be immediately allocated to it ____________

options.text: then the process waits for the resources be allocated to it
the process keeps sending requests until the resource is allocated to it
the process resumes execution without the resource being allocated to it
then all resources currently being held are preempted

questions.explanation:
The no-preemption condition says that a resource cannot be taken away from a process that holds it. To enforce it, if a process holding resources asks for another resource and cannot be granted it immediately, everything it currently holds must first be preempted and rolled back, and only then may it try again. That is the classic OS/2 or database style rule for eliminating hold and wait.

Why D is correct: Enforcing no preemption means preempting and releasing all resources the process holds.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Waiting while holding resources is exactly the hold-and-wait situation that must be avoided.
- B: Repeatedly requesting is the same as waiting and also risks deadlock.
- C: Letting it proceed without the resource breaks the no-preemption rule.

questions.question: Each request requires that the system consider the _____________ to decide whether the current request can be satisfied or must wait to avoid a future possible deadlock.

options.text: processes that have previously been in the system
resources currently allocated to each process
future requests and releases of each process

questions.explanation:
Deadlock avoidance is safe only if the decision about a request is based on more than the resources free right now, which is the same information deadlock detection uses. An algorithm such as the banker's algorithm simulates what each process will claim and release in the future and checks whether a safe sequence still exists after the request is granted.

Why D is correct: Avoidance works by simulating the future requests and releases of every process.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Available resources alone are exactly what detection uses; avoidance needs more.
- B: Past history of processes is irrelevant to the current claim graph.
- C: Current allocations alone do not reveal whether a deadlock is being created.

questions.question: Given a priori information about the ________ number of resources of each type that maybe requested for each process, it is possible to construct an algorithm that ensures that the system will never enter a deadlock state.
questions.explanation:
In the single-instance case a deadlock is impossible as soon as every process has declared the maximum number of instances of each resource it will ever need, because the sums of the claims then exceed what the system can hold. For multiple-instance systems an equivalent bound is computed from the maximum claims of all processes together. The information needed is therefore the maximum requirement, not the minimum or average.

Why C is correct: Knowing the maximum number of each resource type a process may request is what allows a deadlock-free bound to be constructed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: A minimum claim does not guarantee that all demands can be met.
- B: An average claim proves nothing about the worst case.
- D: An approximate claim cannot be used to guarantee freedom from deadlock.

questions.question: A deadlock avoidance algorithm dynamically examines the __________ to ensure that a circular wait condition can never exist.
questions.explanation:
A deadlock avoidance algorithm keeps a model of which process currently holds which resource instances and which instances are still free, and it re-examines that model on every request. By simulating the possible future claims of each process it guarantees that the circular wait condition never actually arises in the allocation graph.

Why A is correct: The algorithm dynamically examines the resource allocation state.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: System storage state is not the state being examined.
- C: The algorithm is about the allocation state, not about the OS as a whole.
- D: Merely looking at resources without their allocation state is not enough.
questions.reviewReason: Near-duplicate stem of q_0361 (extractionFlags duplicate-stem-of); answered independently as instructed.

questions.question: A system is in a safe state only if there exists a ____________
questions.explanation:
The necessary and sufficient condition for safety is the existence of a safe sequence: an ordering of the processes in which each one can obtain its outstanding claim, finish and release its holdings so that the next process can also finish. Without such a sequence the system may deadlock, so a safe state implies a safe sequence.

Why C is correct: A safe state is defined by the existence of a safe sequence.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Safe allocation is not the defined term.
- B: Safe resource is not the defined term.
- D: Incorrect, the concept has a precise name.

questions.question: The FCFS algorithm is particularly troublesome for ____________
questions.explanation:
FCFS is non-preemptive, so a long CPU-bound job that arrives first blocks every interactive job queued behind it for its whole burst. In a time-sharing system, whose purpose is quick response to many users, that convoy effect is the worst case of all. Batch multiprogramming systems, which care mainly about throughput, tolerate it.

Why C is correct: Time-sharing systems are the ones ruined by the FCFS convoy effect.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Too vague to be the specific trouble spot.
- B: FCFS behaves the same way regardless of processor count.
- D: Multiprogramming systems mainly care about throughput, where FCFS is acceptable.
questions.reviewReason: Near-duplicate stem of q_0312 (extractionFlags duplicate-stem-of), with the option letters permuted; answered independently as instructed.

questions.question: A system has 12 magnetic tape drives and 3 processes : P0, P1, and P2. Process P0 requires 10 tape drives, P1 requires 4 and P2 requires 9 tape drives. Process P0 P1 P2 Maximum needs (process-wise: P0 through P2 top to bottom) 10 4 9 5 2 2 Which of the following sequence is a safe sequence?
questions.code: Currently allocated (process-wise)
questions.explanation:
Total allocated is 5 plus 2 plus 2 = 9, so Available = 12 minus 9 = 3 tape drives, and the remaining needs are P0 = 5, P1 = 2 and P2 = 7. Trying the sequence P1, P0, P2: P1 needs 2 which is within the 3 available, so after it finishes Available becomes 5; P0 then needs exactly 5, which is available, and after P0 finishes Available becomes 10; P2 needs 7, which is within 10. Every process can therefore finish in that order, so P1, P0, P2 is a safe sequence.

Why D is correct: P1 needs 2 of the 3 available, P0 then needs 5 of the 5 released, and P2 needs 7 of the 10, so the sequence completes safely.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: P0 needs 5 drives but only 3 are free at the start.
- B: After P1 only 5 are free and P2 needs 7, so it would block.
- C: P2 needs 7 drives but only 3 are free at the start.

questions.question: The resource allocation graph is not applicable to a resource allocation system ____________

options.text: with multiple instances of each resource type
with a single instance of each resource type
single & multiple instances of each resource type

questions.explanation:
A plain resource-allocation-graph cycle test is valid only when each resource type has a single instance, because then a cycle in the graph is both necessary and sufficient for deadlock. With multiple instances a cycle no longer proves deadlock and a claim-and-request graph with multiple requests per process is needed. Hence the simple graph is not applicable to systems with multiple instances.

Why A is correct: The simple cycle-detection graph works only for single-instance resource types.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: With a single instance of each type the graph is fully applicable.
- C: The method is applicable in the single instance case, so this blanket statement is false.
- D: Incorrect, a definite restriction exists.

questions.question: The Banker's algorithm is _____________ than the resource allocation graph algorithm.
questions.explanation:
The banker's algorithm has to run the safety algorithm, simulating what every process may still claim and release, before it can grant any request, and it has to redo that computation for each subsequent request. The resource-allocation-graph approach needs only a graph search, so the banker's algorithm is the more expensive and hence the less efficient of the two.

Why A is correct: Repeatedly simulating future claims makes the banker's algorithm less efficient than a graph based test.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: The banker's algorithm is the costlier one, not the cheaper one.
- C: Their costs differ substantially.
- D: Incorrect, a clear comparison exists.

questions.question: A system with 5 processes P0 through P4 and three resource types A, B, C have A with 10 instances, B with 5 instances, and C with 7 instances. At time t0, the following snapshot has been taken: Process P0 P1 P2 P3 P4 Allocation (process-wise : P0 through P4 top TO bottom) A B C 0 1 0 2 0 0 3 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 2 MAX (process-wise: P0 through P4 top TO bottom) A B C 7 5 3 3 2 2 9 0 2 2 2 2 4 3 3 Available A B C 3 3 2 The sequence <P1, P3, P4, P2, P0> leads the system to ____________
questions.explanation:
Allocated totals are A = 7, B = 2, C = 5, which matches Available of 3, 3, 2 against the totals 10, 5, 7, so the table is read correctly. The remaining needs are P0 = 7,4,3; P1 = 1,2,2; P2 = 6,0,0; P3 = 0,1,3; P4 = 3,3,1. Running the sequence P1, P3, P4, P2, P0 from Available = 3,3,2: P1 needs 1,2,2 and can proceed, releasing 2,0,0 so Available becomes 5,3,2; P3 then needs 0,1,3 and its demand for C of 3 exceeds the 2 available, so the sequence cannot be completed and the state reached is unsafe.

Why A is correct: The sequence fails at P3, whose need of 3 instances of C exceeds the 2 available, so it leads to an unsafe state.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: A safe sequence such as P1, P4, P3, P2, P0 does exist, but the sequence given here is not it.
- C: Protected state is not a defined state of the banker's algorithm.
- D: The system is not necessarily deadlocked; an unsafe state only means deadlock is possible.

questions.question: The wait-for graph is a deadlock detection algorithm that is applicable when ____________

options.text: all resources have a single instance

questions.explanation:
A wait-for graph is obtained from the resource-allocation graph only when every resource type has at most one instance, so each resource can be reduced to a single edge between the holder and the requester. When a resource type has several instances, a cycle in the wait-for graph is only a necessary condition for deadlock, so the reduction algorithm applied to the resource-allocation graph is used instead.

Why A is correct: the wait-for graph detection method applies when all resources have a single instance.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "all resources have multiple instances" is precisely the case the wait-for graph does not handle correctly.
- C: identical wording to option B, so it is wrong for the same reason.
- D: "all" is false, since the method breaks down for multiple instances.
questions.reviewReason: Options B and C are word-for-word identical ("all resources have multiple instances"), so the option set is defective; A is the only distinct statement and is the intended answer.

questions.question: An edge from process Pi to Pj in a wait for graph indicates that ____________

options.text: Pi is waiting for Pj to release a resource that Pi needs
Pi is waiting for Pj to release a resource that Pi needs

questions.explanation:
In a wait-for graph each node is a process, and an edge Pi -> Pj is drawn only when Pi has requested a resource that is currently held by Pj. The arrow therefore runs from the blocked (requesting) process to the owning process that must release the resource.

Why A is correct: an edge Pi to Pj means Pi is waiting for Pj to release a resource that Pi needs.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: identical wording to option A, so it states the same true thing twice.
- C: "all resources have multiple instances" belongs to a different question and says nothing about edge direction.
- D: "all" is false, because option C is meaningless here.
questions.reviewReason: Options A and B are word-for-word identical, so two option keys carry the same correct statement.

questions.question: If the wait for graph contains a cycle ____________

options.text: then a deadlock does not exist
either deadlock exists or system is in a safe state

questions.explanation:
With single-instance resources a cycle in the wait-for graph is equivalent to a deadlock: every process on the cycle is blocked waiting for a resource held by the next process on the cycle, so none of them can ever proceed. The converse also holds, which is why the absence of a cycle proves that no deadlock exists.

Why B is correct: a cycle in the wait-for graph means a deadlock exists.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "then a deadlock does not exist" states the opposite of the standard rule.
- C: "hen a deadlock exists" is a truncated duplicate of option B and means the same thing.
- D: "either deadlock exists or system is in a safe state" only applies to the resource-allocation graph when a resource type has multiple instances, not to the wait-for graph.
questions.reviewReason: Option C is a truncated copy of option B ("hen" is a lost "T"), so two keys carry the same correct statement; B is given as the properly spelled one.

questions.question: If deadlocks occur frequently, the detection algorithm must be invoked ________
questions.explanation:
Detection costs CPU time, so the OS trades detection overhead against how long a deadlocked set wastes resources and blocks everything behind it. When deadlocks occur frequently they must be discovered quickly, because invoking the detection algorithm only rarely would leave deadlocked processes in place for long stretches.

Why B is correct: frequent deadlocks call for invoking the detection algorithm frequently.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "rarely" would let deadlocked processes linger and block others.
- C: "rarely & frequently" is self-contradictory.
- D: "none" is false, the question has a definite answer.

questions.question: For an effective operating system, when to check for deadlock?

options.text: every time a resource request is made
every time a resource request is made at fixed time intervals

questions.explanation:
Running detection on every resource request would make the search cost dominate the real work, so the standard design is to invoke the detection algorithm periodically, at fixed time intervals such as once a second. This bounds how long a deadlock can persist while keeping detection overhead tolerable.

Why A is correct: the detection algorithm is invoked at fixed time intervals.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "every time a resource request is made" is far too expensive because each request triggers a full search.
- C: "every time a resource request is made at fixed time intervals" is a garbled mash-up of the other two options and is self-contradictory.
- D: "none" is false.
questions.reviewReason: Widely circulated answer keys for this exact item select option C ("every time a resource request is made at fixed time intervals"), but that wording is self-contradictory; the textbook rule is periodic invocation at fixed time intervals, so A is given here.

questions.question: What is the main function of the command interpreter?

options.text: to provide the interface between the API and application program
to handle the files in the operating system
to get and execute the next user-specified command

questions.explanation:
The command interpreter, usually the shell, is a system program that reads a user command, decides whether it is a built-in command or the name of a program, and carries it out. Fetching and running that next user-specified command is its entire job.

Why C is correct: "to get and execute the next user-specified command" is exactly the role of the command interpreter.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "to provide the interface between the API and application program" describes the system-call or library layer, not the shell.
- B: "to handle the files in the operating system" is the job of the file system.
- D: "None" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: A deadlock avoidance algorithm dynamically examines the __________ to ensure that a circular wait condition can never exist.
questions.explanation:
Avoidance differs from prevention in that it makes a decision at run time about each individual request, using the current resource-allocation state, that is the available, allocation and maximum-need vectors. By simulating the grant and confirming the system stays in a safe state, algorithms such as Banker's ensure a circular wait never actually forms.

Why D is correct: the term the textbook uses is "resource allocation state".

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "operating system" is far too broad; avoidance inspects one specific data structure.
- B: "resources" is too vague; the full allocation state is required, not the resource list.
- C: "system storage state" is not a term used for deadlock avoidance.
questions.reviewReason: extractionFlags mark this as duplicate-stem-of:q_0348, which lies outside this shard; answered independently as instructed.

questions.question: Swapping _______ be done when a process has pending I/O, or has to execute I/O operations only into operating system buffers.
questions.explanation:
Swapping copies a process's entire memory image out to disk and later restores it, so any outstanding device request would still be pointing at an address whose contents are no longer in memory. For that reason a process that has pending I/O, or one whose I/O writes only into operating-system buffers, must not be swapped.

Why A is correct: swapping must never be performed in this situation.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "maybe" understates the rule, the condition is prohibitive rather than optional.
- C: "can" would invalidate any I/O still in flight.
- D: "must" is the opposite of the correct statement.

questions.question: The main memory accommodates ____________
questions.explanation:
Main memory is split so that the resident portion holds the kernel and the rest holds the running user programs. Among the choices offered, the operating system is unambiguously the resident occupant of main memory for the whole session, which is the statement this item is keyed on.

Why C is correct: the operating system is accommodated in main memory.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "cpu" is wrong, the processor is a separate hardware unit and does not sit in main memory.
- B: "user processes" is also genuinely true of main memory, which makes the option set ambiguous.
- D: "all" is wrong because it drags in the CPU.
questions.reviewReason: Option B (user processes) is also factually true of main memory, and the natural answer would be D "all" if it did not wrongly include the CPU; C is the keyed answer.

questions.question: The operating system is responsible for?
questions.explanation:
The operating system owns the storage hardware and its failure handling: it runs the boot program to bring the system up from disk, formats and initialises disks, and maps bad blocks onto spare blocks whenever a disk error occurs. All three of the listed jobs are therefore OS responsibilities.

Why D is correct: bad-block recovery, booting from disk and disk initialization are all handled by the operating system.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "bad-block recovery" is true but covers only one of the three jobs.
- B: "booting from disk" is true but covers only one of the three jobs.
- C: "disk initialization" is true but covers only one of the three jobs.

questions.question: The operating system and the other processes are protected from being modified by an already running process because ____________

options.text: every address generated by the CPU is being checked against the relocation and limit registers
they are in different memory spaces
they are in different logical addresses

questions.explanation:
In the relocation-register scheme the OS loads a base register with the lowest physical address of the process and a limit register with the extent of its logical address space. Hardware checks every logical address the CPU generates against the limit and then adds the base, so any address outside the process's own range traps before it can touch the kernel or another process.

Why A is correct: every CPU-generated address is checked against the relocation and limit registers.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "they have a protection algorithm" names no real mechanism; the protection is in hardware.
- C: "they are in different memory spaces" is false, all processes share one physical memory.
- D: "they are in different logical addresses" is true of every process, so it cannot be the distinguishing reason.

questions.question: Using transient code, _______ the size of the operating system during program execution.
questions.explanation:
Transient operating-system code and data, such as device drivers or utilities, are loaded into memory only when needed and unloaded when no longer required. Because the resident kernel therefore grows and shrinks at run time instead of staying a fixed size, using transient code changes the size of the operating system during program execution.

Why B is correct: the OS size "changes" as transient code is loaded and unloaded.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "maintains" would require a fixed resident size, which is exactly what transient code avoids.
- C: "increases" ignores that the code is also unloaded again.
- D: "decreases" suggests a one-way shrink, whereas the size fluctuates.

questions.question: The operating system maintains a ______ table that keeps track of how many frames have been allocated, how many are there, and how many are available.
questions.explanation:
Physical memory is divided into fixed-size frames, and the OS keeps a frame table, usually realised as a free-frame list, recording for every frame whether it is free and how many frames exist in total. The page table is a different structure: it belongs to a process and maps that process's pages to frames.

Why D is correct: it is the frame table that tracks allocated, total and available frames.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "memory" is too generic, there is no table simply called memory.
- B: "mapping" tables are page tables or segment tables, which map logical to physical addresses.
- C: "page" tables count a process's pages, not the frames of physical memory.

questions.question: To obtain better memory utilization, dynamic loading is used. With dynamic loading, a routine is not loaded until it is called. For implementing dynamic loading ____________

options.text: special support from operating system is essential
special support from hardware is required
user programs can implement dynamic loading without any special support from hardware or operating system
special support from both hardware and operating system is essential

questions.explanation:
Dynamic loading differs from dynamic linking in that the program itself decides when to bring in a routine, normally by calling a stub that reads the routine from secondary storage and jumps to it. That is purely a software technique and requires neither paging hardware nor any help from the kernel.

Why C is correct: user programs implement dynamic loading without special hardware or operating-system support.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "special support from operating system is essential" is false, no OS support is needed.
- B: "special support from hardware is required" is false, no hardware support is needed.
- D: "special support from both hardware and operating system is essential" is false on both counts.

questions.question: The _________ presents a uniform device-access interface to the I/O subsystem, much as system calls provide a standard interface between the application and the operating system.
questions.explanation:
A device driver encapsulates the specifics of one controller and translates generic requests such as read and write into device commands, so that all devices look alike to the kernel and to applications. This is exactly parallel to system calls presenting one standard interface between the application and the operating system.

Why A is correct: Device drivers present a uniform device-access interface to the I/O subsystem.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "I/O systems" is the whole layer being presented, not the presenting interface.
- C: "Devices" are physical units and cannot present an interface.
- D: "Buses" merely carry signals between components.

questions.question: In real time operating system ____________

options.text: process scheduling can be done only once
all processes have the same priority
a task must be serviced by its deadline period

questions.explanation:
A real-time OS is defined by timing guarantees rather than by fairness or throughput. It must guarantee that every task is serviced within its deadline, whether that is an absolute or a relative deadline, and missing a deadline counts as a functional failure rather than merely a delay.

Why D is correct: a task must be serviced by its deadline period.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "process scheduling can be done only once" is false, scheduling recurs constantly.
- B: "all processes have the same priority" is false, real-time systems use multiple priority levels.
- C: "kernel is not required" is false, a kernel is always present.

questions.question: In Operating Systems, which of the following is/are CPU scheduling algorithms?
questions.explanation:
Priority scheduling, round-robin (time-sharing) and shortest-job-first are all standard CPU scheduling policies, and SJF in turn underlies several non-preemptive and preemptive variants. Since every one of the three named policies is a genuine scheduling algorithm, the collective option applies.

Why D is correct: Priority, Round Robin and Shortest Job First are all CPU scheduling algorithms.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Priority" is a real algorithm but accounts for only one of the three.
- B: "Round Robin" is a real algorithm but accounts for only one of the three.
- C: "Shortest Job First" is a real algorithm but accounts for only one of the three.

questions.question: Hard real time operating system has ______________ jitter than a soft real time operating system.
questions.explanation:
Jitter is the variation in the time between successive activations or responses of a periodic task. A hard real-time system must behave deterministically, so its jitter is tightly bounded and therefore smaller than that of a soft real-time system, where occasional long delays are tolerated without penalty.

Why C is correct: hard real-time operating systems have less jitter.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "equal" contradicts the whole point of hard real-time determinism.
- B: "more" is the wrong direction entirely.
- D: "none" is false, since "less" completes the sentence correctly.

questions.question: For real time operating systems, interrupt latency should be ____________
questions.explanation:
Interrupt latency is the delay between the arrival of an interrupt and the start of its service routine, which includes interrupt detection, acknowledgement and dispatch. It can never literally be zero because that hardware and kernel work takes real time, but a real-time OS must drive it as low as it can so that deadlines are still met.

Why B is correct: interrupt latency should be minimal.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "zero" is physically impossible, detection and dispatch consume time.
- C: "maximum" is the opposite of the requirement.
- D: "dependent on the scheduling" is wrong, latency is a hardware and kernel response time, not a scheduling decision.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a real time operating system?
questions.explanation:
RTLinux is a real-time extension of Linux, VxWorks is a dedicated real-time OS, and Windows CE targets embedded hand-held devices with priority-based, bounded-latency scheduling and is listed among real-time operating systems in the standard textbook table. All three therefore qualify.

Why D is correct: Windows CE, RTLinux and VxWorks are all real-time operating systems.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Windows CE" is an RTOS but covers only one of the three.
- B: "RTLinux" is an RTOS but covers only one of the three.
- C: "VxWorks" is an RTOS but covers only one of the three.

questions.question: The priority of a process will ______________ if the scheduler assigns it a static priority.
questions.explanation:
A static priority is assigned once, normally when the process is created or admitted, and the scheduler never recomputes it. That is the whole contrast with a dynamic or ageing priority, which is boosted while a process waits so that it cannot be starved.

Why C is correct: a static priority remains unchanged.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "depends on the operating system" is unnecessary, the word "static" already fixes the behaviour.
- B: "change" would describe a dynamic priority.
- D: "none" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: If the sum of the working set sizes increases, exceeding the total number of available frames ____________

options.text: the operating system selects a process to suspend

questions.explanation:
If the sum of the working-set sizes of all processes exceeds the number of available frames, thrashing sets in: pages are faulted in and evicted faster than the processes can complete useful work. The standard working-set remedy is to suspend one of the processes so the aggregate working set fits within the frames available.

Why A is correct: the operating system selects a process to suspend.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "the system crashes" is wrong, thrashing degrades performance without crashing.
- C: "then the process crashes" is wrong, no process is terminated by thrashing.
- D: "the memory overflows" is wrong, frames are simply over-subscribed.

questions.question: The information about all files is kept in ____________
questions.explanation:
The operating system keeps a directory structure that is logically separate from the file data, and in that structure each file's name, location, owner and type are recorded. That directory is therefore the place where the information about all files is held.

Why B is correct: the information about all files is kept in a separate directory structure.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "operating system" is far too broad, the OS holds many structures and this names none of them.
- C: "swap space" holds swapped-out process images, not file information.
- D: "none" is false, because option B is correct.

questions.question: The operating system keeps a small table containing information about all open files called ____________
questions.explanation:
The OS maintains two levels of open-file tables: a small per-process table of file descriptors, and a single system-wide open-file table with one entry per open file holding the read/write pointers, access rights and location. The structure that keeps information about all open files is therefore the open-file table.

Why C is correct: the open-file table holds information about all open files.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "file table" is not the standard name for this structure.
- B: "directory table" lists the names in a directory, not open files.
- D: "system table" is a generic label, not the defined structure.

questions.question: What will happen in the single level directory?

options.text: All files are contained in the same directory
All files are contained in different directories all at the same level

questions.explanation:
A single-level directory has exactly one directory for the entire system, so every file belonging to every user must be placed in that same directory. Its chief drawback is that two different users cannot own files with the same name, because names must be unique across the one directory.

Why A is correct: all files are contained in the same directory.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "All files are contained in different directories all at the same level" describes a two-level, per-user directory structure.
- C: "Depends on the operating system" is wrong, the structure is defined by the scheme itself.
- D: "None" is false, because option A is correct.

questions.question: The operating system _______ the links when traversing directory trees, to preserve the acyclic structure of the system.
questions.explanation:
Symbolic, or soft, links can point anywhere in the file system and can therefore close a loop back onto an ancestor, turning the tree into a graph containing a cycle. To preserve the acyclic structure the operating system ignores such links while walking the directory structure, which is what stops a traversal from looping forever.

Why C is correct: the operating system ignores the offending links when traversing directory trees.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "deletes" would destroy valid user data during a mere directory walk.
- B: "considers" is exactly what would allow the cycle to be followed.
- D: "none" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: On systems where there are multiple operating system, the decision to load a particular one is done by _____________
questions.explanation:
Bootstrap code held in ROM only brings the hardware far enough up to read the boot sector; the component that reads that sector and decides which operating-system image or kernel to load is the boot loader. The choice between multiple installed operating systems is therefore made by the boot loader.

Why C is correct: the boot loader decides which operating system to load.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "process control block" describes a running process, not the boot decision.
- B: "file control block" describes an open file.
- D: "bootstrap" initialises hardware and then hands over to the boot loader.

questions.question: To access the services of the operating system, the interface is provided by the ___________
questions.explanation:
A system call is the controlled, privileged entry point through which a user program asks the kernel for a service such as file access, process creation or memory. System calls are therefore the interface by which applications reach the services of the operating system.

Why B is correct: System Calls provide the interface to operating-system services.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Library" is a collection of routines, some of which merely wrap system calls.
- C: "Assembly instructions" refers to the few privileged instructions that trigger the trap, not to the user-level interface.
- D: "API - Application Programming Interface" is the higher-level abstraction layered on top, not the mechanism of access.

questions.question: The _______ program initializes all aspects of the system, from CPU registers to device controllers and the contents of main memory, and then starts the operating system.
questions.explanation:
The bootstrap program is the small routine held in ROM that runs at power-on: it initialises the CPU registers, the device controllers and the contents of main memory, locates and loads the operating system, and transfers control to it. That is precisely what the question describes.

Why A is correct: the bootstrap program initialises all aspects of the system and starts the OS.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "main" is an application's C entry point and has nothing to do with booting.
- C: "bootloader" loads the OS, but the full hardware initialisation described belongs to the bootstrap.
- D: "rom" is storage hardware, not a program.

questions.question: Network operating system runs on ___________

options.text: both server and every system in the network

questions.explanation:
In the network operating-system model the shared resources such as files, printers and user accounts are managed centrally, and the system software that actually provides those services runs on the machine that owns them, which is the server. Machines elsewhere in the network act as clients and reach that software through the network protocol.

Why B is correct: the network operating system runs on the server.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "every system in the network" is wrong, clients run only client stubs, not the NOS itself.
- C: "both server and every system in the network" double-counts, since the server is itself one of the systems in the network.
- D: "none" is false, because option B is correct.

questions.question: What are the types of distributed operating systems?
questions.explanation:
Of the three categories listed, only the network operating system is a recognised member of the distributed-systems taxonomy, in which a single unified view of shared resources is offered across networked machines. "Zone based" and "level based" operating systems are not standard classifications of distributed operating systems.

Why C is correct: Network Operating system is a valid type of distributed operating system.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Zone based Operating system" is not a recognised type of distributed operating system.
- B: "Level based Operating system" is not a recognised type of distributed operating system.
- D: "All" is false, because two of the listed items are not types of distributed OS.

questions.question: The systems which allow only one process execution at a time, are called __________
questions.explanation:
Uniprocessing means the machine has a single processor, and in the single-process form of such a system only one process may execute at any instant while all others wait their turn for the CPU. Strictly speaking the term that means one program resident in memory is uniprogramming, so the wording of the question and its keyed answer are not fully consistent.

Why B is correct: the intended key for this item is "uniprocessing systems".

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "uniprogramming systems" is the term that actually means a single program in memory, so it is also defensible.
- C: "unitasking systems" refers to a process executing one task at a time, not to single-process execution.
- D: "none" is false, because option B is the intended answer.
questions.reviewReason: Options A ("uniprogramming systems") and B ("uniprocessing systems") are both defensible readings of the stem; B is the key used by this source bank while A is the technically precise term.

questions.question: In operating system, each process has its own __________

options.text: pending alarms, signals and signal handlers

questions.explanation:
Each process owns a protected address space holding its code, data, stack and heap together with its globals, it has its own list of open files, and it has its own pending alarms, signals and signal handlers. All three statements are therefore true of every process.

Why D is correct: address space and globals, open files, and pending alarms and signals all belong to a process.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "address space and global variables" is true but is only part of the answer.
- B: "open files" is true but is only part of the answer.
- C: "pending alarms, signals and signal handlers" is true but is only part of the answer.
questions.reviewReason: extractionFlags mark this as duplicate-stem-of:q_0284, which lies outside this shard; answered independently as instructed.

questions.question: A process can be terminated due to __________
questions.explanation:
A process ends either normally when its main routine returns or exit() is called, abnormally when it encounters a fatal error, or forcibly when another process or the user kills it. The OS reclaims the process's resources in every one of those cases.

Why D is correct: normal exit, fatal error and being killed by another process are all reasons a process can terminate.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "normal exit" is only one of the three causes.
- B: "fatal error" is only one of the three causes.
- C: "killed by another process" is only one of the three causes.

questions.question: What is the ready state of a process?

options.text: when process is scheduled to run after some execution
when process is unable to run until some task has been completed
when process is using the CPU

questions.explanation:
The ready state means the process is sitting in the ready queue: it already holds everything it needs to execute and is waiting only for the CPU. Option A describes exactly that situation for a process that has finished some earlier execution and is now waiting to be dispatched again.

Why A is correct: the process is ready to be scheduled to run after some execution.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "when process is unable to run until some task has been completed" is the blocked or waiting state.
- C: "when process is using the CPU" is the running state.
- D: "none" is false, because option A is the intended answer.

questions.question: What is interprocess communication?

options.text: communication between two threads of same process

questions.explanation:
IPC is the set of mechanisms by which separate processes, which do not share an address space, exchange data and coordinate their relative order of execution. Communication inside a single process, or between threads of one process, is ordinary shared-memory programming rather than IPC.

Why B is correct: interprocess communication is communication between two processes.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "communication within the process" is internal to one process, so it is not IPC.
- C: "communication between two threads of same process" shares one address space, so it is not IPC.
- D: "none" is false, because option B is correct.
questions.reviewReason: extractionFlags mark this as duplicate-stem-of:q_0441, which is also in this shard; both entries were answered independently as instructed.

questions.question: A set of processes is deadlock if __________

options.text: each process is blocked and will remain so forever
all processes are trying to kill each other

questions.explanation:
A set of processes is deadlocked when every member is blocked, each waiting for an event that only another member of the set can produce, so none of them can ever run again and none can release what the others need. That is precisely the condition of every process being blocked and remaining so forever.

Why A is correct: each process being blocked forever is the definition of deadlock.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "each process is terminated" describes finished processes, not deadlocked ones.
- C: "all processes are trying to kill each other" is not the definition.
- D: "None" is false, because option A is correct.

questions.question: A process stack does not contain __________
questions.explanation:
A stack frame holds the parameters of the active call, the local or automatic variables of that call, and the return address back to the caller. Process identifiers such as the PID of a child are recorded in the process control block and the process table instead, not on the stack.

Why D is correct: the PID of a child process is not contained in the process stack.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Function parameters" are pushed onto the stack for every call.
- B: "Local variables" are allocated on the stack.
- C: "Return addresses" are stored on the stack to unwind the call chain.

questions.question: CPU scheduling is the basis of ___________
questions.explanation:
Multiprogramming only pays off if the OS can switch the CPU between processes: while one is blocked on I/O another is dispatched to run. Without CPU scheduling the single running process would leave the CPU idle for the whole duration of its I/O, which is precisely what the technique exists to prevent.

Why A is correct: CPU scheduling is the basis of multiprogramming operating systems.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "larger memory sized systems" is a precondition for multiprogramming, not what scheduling is based on.
- C: "multiprocessor systems" need multiprocessor scheduling and are not the basis of multiprogramming.
- D: "none" is false, because option A is correct.
questions.reviewReason: extractionFlags mark this as duplicate-stem-of:q_0282, which lies outside this shard; answered independently as instructed.

questions.question: Which system call can be used by a parent process to determine the termination of child process?
questions.explanation:
The wait() call blocks the calling parent until one of its children terminates and then returns that child's exit status and PID, which is exactly how a parent learns that the child has finished. fork() creates a child and returns immediately, and exit() is called by the terminating child itself.

Why A is correct: wait() lets the parent determine the termination of its child.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "exit" is called by the child to terminate itself, not by the parent to observe it.
- C: "fork" creates a new child process.
- D: "get" is not a standard process-related system call.

questions.question: The address of the next instruction to be executed by the current process is provided by the __________
questions.explanation:
The program counter holds the address of the instruction currently executing and is incremented after each instruction, so it always holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched. Its value is saved in the PCB on every context switch so execution can resume in the right place.

Why B is correct: the Program counter provides the address of the next instruction to be executed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "CPU registers" is a set of registers, not the specific holder of the next instruction address.
- C: "Process stack" holds local variables, parameters and return addresses.
- D: "Pipe" is an IPC mechanism and has nothing to do with the instruction address.

questions.question: A Process Control Block(PCB) does not contain which of the following?
questions.explanation:
A PCB records identification data such as the PID, the process state, the program counter and CPU registers, scheduling information, memory-management data, and pointers or limits describing the process's code, data and stack. The bootstrap program is part of the fixed system image and has nothing to do with any individual process.

Why C is correct: the Bootstrap Program is not contained in a PCB.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Code" is referenced by the PCB through the code segment pointer.
- B: "Stack" is described by the stack pointer and stack limits stored in the PCB.
- D: "Data" is referenced by the PCB through the data segment pointer.

questions.question: The number of processes completed per unit time is known as __________
questions.explanation:
Throughput is defined as the number of processes that complete per unit of time, and it is one of the classic CPU scheduling criteria alongside turnaround time, waiting time and response time. Output, efficiency and capacity are not the names of this metric.

Why B is correct: processes completed per unit time is Throughput.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Output" is not a scheduling performance metric.
- C: "Efficiency" is the fraction of time the CPU is busy, which is a different criterion.
- D: "Capacity" is not a scheduling performance metric.

questions.question: The state of a process is defined by __________

options.text: the current activity of the process
the final activity of the process
the activity just executed by the process
the activity to next be executed by the process

questions.explanation:
A process state such as new, ready, running, waiting or terminated is simply the activity the process is currently engaged in during its life cycle. It is not defined by what the process did last, nor by the instruction it will execute next.

Why A is correct: the state of a process is its current activity.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "the final activity of the process" is about termination, not state.
- C: "the activity just executed by the process" describes history, not current state.
- D: "the activity to next be executed by the process" describes the next instruction, not the process state.

questions.question: Which of the following is not the state of a process?
questions.explanation:
The canonical set of process states is new, ready, running, waiting (blocked) and terminated. "Old" is not a member of that model, so it is the odd one out in this list.

Why B is correct: "Old" is not one of the states of a process.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "New" is a standard process state.
- C: "Waiting" is a standard process state.
- D: "Running" is a standard process state.

questions.question: What is a Process Control Block?
questions.explanation:
The PCB is the kernel's data structure in which every piece of information the OS needs about a process is recorded, which is what allows a process to be suspended and later resumed exactly where it left off. It is not a variable, not a region of secondary storage, and not merely an arbitrary block of memory.

Why B is correct: a Process Control Block is a Data Structure.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Process type variable" is not a real entity.
- C: "A secondary storage section" is wrong, PCBs live in kernel main memory.
- D: "A Block in memory" is true but far too vague to be the definition.

questions.question: The entry of all the PCBs of the current processes is in __________
questions.explanation:
The OS keeps a process table, which is an array of pointers to the PCBs of every process currently in the system, and that is what lets the kernel find a process's control block from a PID. Neither a CPU register nor a program counter can hold such a list.

Why C is correct: the entries of all the current PCBs are held in the Process Table.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Process Register" is a CPU register holding one context, not a table.
- B: "Program Counter" holds a single address.
- D: "Process Unit" is not a real structure in an operating system.

questions.question: What is the degree of multiprogramming?

options.text: the number of processes executed per unit time
the number of processes in the ready queue
the number of processes in the I/O queue
the number of processes in memory

questions.explanation:
The degree of multiprogramming is the number of processes that are resident in main memory at a given moment, which bounds how many can compete for the CPU and how much memory the OS must hold at once. Processes completed per unit time is instead the definition of throughput.

Why D is correct: it is the number of processes in memory.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "the number of processes executed per unit time" is throughput.
- B: "the number of processes in the ready queue" is a momentary count, not the degree of multiprogramming.
- C: "the number of processes in the I/O queue" is unrelated to the degree of multiprogramming.

questions.question: A single thread of control allows the process to perform __________

options.text: only one task at a time
only two tasks at a time

questions.explanation:
A thread of control is a single sequential path of execution with its own program counter, register set and stack. With only one such path a process can make progress on exactly one task at a time, and genuine simultaneity requires several threads.

Why A is correct: a single thread of control lets the process perform only one task at a time.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "multiple tasks at a time" requires more than one thread.
- C: "only two tasks at a time" is arbitrary and false.
- D: "all" is false because options B and C are both wrong.

questions.question: Which one of the following is not true?

options.text: kernel remains in the memory during the entire computer session
kernel is made of various modules which can not be loaded in running operating system
kernel is the first part of the operating system to load into memory during booting
kernel is the program that constitutes the central core of the operating system

questions.explanation:
Three of the four statements are true: the kernel stays resident in memory, it is the central core of the operating system, and it is the first part of the OS loaded during booting. The false one is the claim that its modules can never be loaded into a running system, since modern kernels do load and unload modules dynamically at run time.

Why B is correct: it is false, kernel modules can be loaded into a running operating system.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "kernel remains in the memory during the entire computer session" is true.
- C: "kernel is the first part of the operating system to load into memory during booting" is true.
- D: "kernel is the program that constitutes the central core of the operating system" is true.

questions.question: What is the objective of multiprogramming?

options.text: Have a process running at all time
Have multiple programs waiting in a queue ready to run

questions.explanation:
Multiprogramming keeps several processes in memory so that whenever one is blocked on I/O the CPU can be handed to another instead of idling. The purpose of that arrangement is to raise CPU utilisation, which is why utilisation is the headline objective of the technique.

Why C is correct: the objective of multiprogramming is to increase CPU utilization.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Have a process running at all time" is a consequence of the objective rather than the stated aim.
- B: "Have multiple programs waiting in a queue ready to run" describes the ready queue, not the objective.
- D: "None" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: Which of the following do not belong to queues for processes?
questions.explanation:
The standard queueing model of a multiprogrammed system contains the job queue, the ready queue and one device queue for each I/O device. A PCB is a record attached to a process rather than a queue of waiting entities, so it does not belong in that list.

Why B is correct: PCB Queue does not belong to queues for processes.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Job Queue" is a genuine process queue.
- C: "Device Queue" is a genuine process queue.
- D: "Ready Queue" is a genuine process queue.

questions.question: When the process issues an I/O request __________

options.text: It is placed in an I/O queue
It is placed in a waiting queue
It is placed in the ready queue
It is placed in the Job queue

questions.explanation:
When a running process issues an I/O request it cannot continue, so the OS blocks it and links it into the device queue for that device; only when the I/O completes is it moved to the ready queue. The job queue, by contrast, holds jobs that have not yet been admitted to the system at all.

Why A is correct: the process is placed in an I/O queue.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "It is placed in a waiting queue" describes the same outcome in different words, so the option set is not exclusive.
- C: "It is placed in the ready queue" happens only after the I/O completes.
- D: "It is placed in the Job queue" is wrong, that queue holds jobs before admission.
questions.reviewReason: Option B ("placed in a waiting queue") expresses the same outcome as A in different words; A is the term used for the device/I-O queue and is the keyed answer.

questions.question: What will happen when a process terminates?

options.text: It is removed from all queues
It is removed from all, but the job queue
Its process control block is de-allocated
Its process control block is never de-allocated

questions.explanation:
When a process terminates the kernel releases all its resources, removes it from every queue to which it belongs, and frees its PCB, leaving at most a zombie entry until the parent waits. The first observable effect, and the one this item is keyed on, is its removal from all queues.

Why A is correct: a terminating process is removed from all the queues.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "It is removed from all, but the job queue" is wrong, it leaves every queue without exception.
- C: "Its process control block is de-allocated" is also true of termination, so the option set is not exclusive.
- D: "Its process control block is never de-allocated" is false, the PCB is freed or left only as a zombie entry.
questions.reviewReason: Both A and C describe what the textbook says happens on termination (removal from all queues and freeing the PCB), so two options are defensible; A is the keyed answer.

questions.question: What is a long-term scheduler?

options.text: It selects processes which have to be brought into the ready queue
It selects processes which have to be executed next and allocates CPU
It selects processes which heave to remove from memory by swapping

questions.explanation:
The long-term, or job, scheduler chooses which processes from the job queue are admitted to the ready queue, and it runs only occasionally, for instance when the degree of multiprogramming must be changed. Handing the CPU to the next ready process and swapping processes out of memory are the jobs of the short- and medium-term schedulers.

Why A is correct: the long-term scheduler selects processes to bring into the ready queue.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "It selects processes which have to be executed next and allocates CPU" is the short-term scheduler.
- C: "It selects processes which heave to remove from memory by swapping" is the medium-term scheduler.
- D: "None" is false, because option A is correct.

questions.question: If all processes I/O bound, the ready queue will almost always be ______ and the Short term Scheduler will have a ______ to do.
questions.explanation:
An I/O-bound process spends the great majority of its time blocked on a device, so processes leave the ready queue almost as fast as they enter it and very few are waiting to run. The ready queue is therefore almost empty, which leaves the short-term scheduler with little to choose between.

Why C is correct: the ready queue is empty and the scheduler has little to do.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "full, little" describes CPU-bound processes, which is the opposite situation.
- B: "full, lot" contradicts the I/O-bound premise.
- D: "empty, lot" is self-defeating, an empty queue leaves the scheduler nothing to do.

questions.question: What is a medium-term scheduler?

options.text: It selects which process has to be brought into the ready queue
It selects which process has to be executed next and allocates CPU
It selects which process to remove from memory by swapping

questions.explanation:
A medium-term scheduler swaps a process out of memory to suspend it and later swaps it back in, typically to relieve memory pressure or to let a higher-priority process run. It neither admits jobs from the job queue nor dispatches the running process.

Why C is correct: it selects which process to remove from memory by swapping.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "It selects which process has to be brought into the ready queue" is the long-term scheduler.
- B: "It selects which process has to be executed next and allocates CPU" is the short-term scheduler.
- D: "None" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: What is a short-term scheduler?

options.text: It selects which process has to be brought into the ready queue
It selects which process has to be executed next and allocates CPU
It selects which process to remove from memory by swapping

questions.explanation:
The short-term, or CPU, scheduler runs on every interrupt or voluntary yield, picks a process out of the ready queue and dispatches it, thereby allocating the CPU to the next process to execute. Admitting jobs and swapping processes are the long-term and medium-term schedulers' jobs respectively.

Why B is correct: it selects which process is executed next and allocates the CPU.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "It selects which process has to be brought into the ready queue" is the long-term scheduler.
- C: "It selects which process to remove from memory by swapping" is the medium-term scheduler.
- D: "None" is false, because option B is correct.

questions.question: The primary distinction between the short term scheduler and the long term scheduler is __________

options.text: The type of processes they schedule

questions.explanation:
The short-term scheduler must fire on every timer tick or blocking event, while the long-term scheduler runs only occasionally to adjust the degree of multiprogramming. That difference in how often each one runs is what distinguishes them, since both schedule ordinary processes and both operate on queues.

Why C is correct: the distinction is the frequency of their execution.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "The length of their queues" is a consequence of their roles, not the defining difference.
- B: "The type of processes they schedule" is the same for both.
- D: "None" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: The only state transition that is initiated by the user process itself is __________
questions.explanation:
A process moves itself from running to blocked only when it asks for something it cannot have yet, such as an I/O operation, so blocking is the one transition the process initiates by itself. The wake-up is triggered by the event the process was waiting for, and the dispatch is performed by the dispatcher after scheduling.

Why A is correct: block is the only transition the user process itself initiates.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "wakeup" is caused by the awaited event, not by the process.
- C: "dispatch" is performed by the dispatcher after the scheduler decides.
- D: "none" is false, because option A is correct.

questions.question: Which one of the following errors will be handle by the operating system?
questions.explanation:
The OS continuously monitors and recovers from errors it can act on: a paper-out condition is reported by the device driver and surfaced to the process, and a network connection failure is reported by the driver to the socket layer, which returns an error to the application.
