Power failure is likewise handled at the system level through orderly shutdown and recovery on restart, so all three are OS-handled errors.

Why D is correct: all the mentioned errors are handled by the operating system.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "lack of paper in printer" is handled, but it is only one of the three.
- B: "connection failure in the network" is handled, but it is only one of the three.
- C: "power failure" is handled, but it is only one of the three.

questions.question: In a time-sharing operating system, when the time slot given to a process is completed, the process goes from the running state to the __________
questions.explanation:
In a round-robin time-sharing system a process runs until its time quantum expires or until it blocks; when the quantum expires a timer interrupt preempts it and it goes back to the ready queue to wait for its next turn. It is not suspended, since nothing is swapped out, and it is certainly not terminated.

Why B is correct: the process returns to the Ready state when its time slot ends.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Blocked state" is entered only when the process waits for an event such as I/O.
- C: "Suspended state" means swapped out of memory, which does not happen here.
- D: "Suspended state" is a word-for-word duplicate of option C.
questions.reviewReason: Known source defect: options C and D are identical ("Suspended state"); the original fourth option was most likely "Terminated state", but B is correct either way.

questions.question: In a multiprogramming environment __________

options.text: the processor executes more than one process at a time
the programs are developed by more than one person
more than one process resides in the memory
a single user can execute many programs at the same time

questions.explanation:
Multiprogramming means keeping several processes resident in main memory at once; the single CPU still executes only one of them at any instant and the OS switches between them as one blocks. Option A would describe true parallelism on multiple cores, not multiprogramming.

Why C is correct: more than one process resides in the memory.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "the processor executes more than one process at a time" is false, one CPU runs one process at a time.
- B: "the programs are developed by more than one person" is unrelated to multiprogramming.
- D: "a single user can execute many programs at the same time" describes the user's view of time sharing, not the definition.

questions.question: Suppose that a process is in "Blocked" state waiting for some I/O service. When the service is completed, it goes to the __________
questions.explanation:
Once the awaited I/O completes the blocking condition disappears, so the OS unblocks the process and puts it in the ready queue. It reaches running only later, when the scheduler dispatches it, which is why a process never jumps straight from waiting to running.

Why B is correct: the process moves to the Ready state.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Running state" is wrong, a blocked process must pass through ready first.
- C: "Suspended state" is wrong, nothing is swapped out here.
- D: "Terminated state" is wrong, completing an I/O does not end the process.

questions.question: The context of a process in the PCB of a process does not contain __________

options.text: the value of the CPU registers

questions.explanation:
The process context stored in the PCB comprises the values of the CPU registers including the program counter, the process state, and memory-management information such as the page-table base and the addressing limits. Context switch time is a cost incurred while switching, not part of any process's saved context.

Why D is correct: context switch time is not part of the stored context.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "the value of the CPU registers" is saved as part of the context.
- B: "the process state" is part of the context.
- C: "memory-management information" is part of the context.

questions.question: Which of the following need not necessarily be saved on a context switch between processes?
questions.explanation:
On a context switch the OS saves the general-purpose registers and the program counter, because those values belong to the outgoing process and are needed to resume it. The TLB is part of the MMU and is normally flushed or simply refilled by the hardware, so it need not be saved as process context.

Why B is correct: the Translation lookaside buffer need not necessarily be saved.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "General purpose registers" must be saved or the process cannot resume correctly.
- C: "Program counter" must be saved or the process resumes at the wrong instruction.
- D: "All" is false, since registers and the program counter must be saved.

questions.question: Which of the following does not interrupt a running process?
questions.explanation:
An I/O device raises an interrupt when it needs service, the timer raises one on every quantum expiry to drive preemption, and a power failure also generates an interrupt so the OS can halt safely. The scheduler itself interrupts nothing: it is invoked after an interrupt or a yield and simply chooses which process to dispatch next.

Why C is correct: the Schedular process does not interrupt a running process.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "A device" interrupts, which is the classic interrupt-driven I/O case.
- B: "Timer" interrupts, driving round-robin preemption of the running process.
- D: "Power Failure" also generates an interrupt.

questions.question: Which process can be affected by other processes executing in the system?
questions.explanation:
A cooperating process is one that shares data with, or otherwise communicates with, another process, so it can be affected by what that other process does and can equally affect it in turn. An ordinary child, an ordinary parent or the init process only stands in a hierarchical relationship and is not by definition influenced by other running processes.

Why A is correct: a cooperating process can be affected by other processes executing in the system.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "child process" shares a parent-child relationship, which is not mutual interference.
- C: "parent process" shares the same relationship, not mutual interference.
- D: "init process" is the root of the process tree, not a shared-resource process.

questions.question: When several processes access the same data concurrently and the outcome of the execution depends on the particular order in which the access takes place is called ________
questions.explanation:
A race condition arises when two or more concurrent processes access shared data without synchronisation and the resulting value depends on the unpredictable order in which the accesses occur. The remedy is to guard the shared data with mutual exclusion, and the guarded region is called the critical section.

Why B is correct: this is precisely a race condition.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "dynamic condition" is not a defined term.
- C: "essential condition" is not a defined term.
- D: "critical condition" is not a defined term.

questions.question: If a process is executing in its critical section, then no other processes can be executing in their critical section. What is this condition called?
questions.explanation:
Mutual exclusion is the requirement that at most one process at a time may be executing inside the critical section, so every other process must wait its turn. That is exactly the condition described in the question.

Why A is correct: the condition is called mutual exclusion.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "critical exclusion" is not a recognised term.
- C: "synchronous exclusion" is not a recognised term.
- D: "asynchronous exclusion" is not a recognised term.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a synchronization tool?
questions.explanation:
A semaphore is the classic synchronisation primitive: an integer manipulated only through the atomic wait and signal operations, used to control entry to a critical section. Pipes, sockets and threads are communication or scheduling constructs rather than the synchronisation tool the question is asking for.

Why C is correct: semaphore is the synchronisation tool.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "thread" is a unit of execution, not a synchronisation primitive.
- B: "pipe" is an IPC mechanism.
- D: "socket" is an IPC endpoint.

questions.question: Where is the operating system placed in the memory?

options.text: either low or high memory (depending on the location of interrupt vector)

questions.explanation:
The OS image can be linked at either end of physical memory depending on where the interrupt-vector table is placed: when the vector occupies low memory the OS is loaded at high memory, and the reverse when the vector is high. The placement therefore depends on the interrupt-vector location rather than on a fixed convention.

Why A is correct: the OS goes in low or high memory depending on the location of the interrupt vector.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "in the low memory" holds only when the interrupt vector is in high memory.
- C: "in the high memory" holds only when the interrupt vector is in low memory.
- D: "none" is false, because option A is correct.

questions.question: A semaphore is a shared integer variable __________

options.text: that can not drop below zero
that can not be more than zero
that can not drop below one
that can not be more than one

questions.explanation:
In the usual presentation the semaphore starts at 1 for a binary lock or at the number of free units for a counting semaphore; signal increments it and wait decrements it, so the value is not driven below zero and a value of zero means no unit is free. Note that in Dijkstra's original formulation a counting semaphore may legitimately take negative values, so the wording here is a simplification.

Why A is correct: the intended statement is that a semaphore cannot drop below zero.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "that can not be more than zero" is wrong, a semaphore is positive when resources are free.
- C: "that can not drop below one" is wrong, a binary semaphore legitimately sits at 0.
- D: "that can not be more than one" is wrong, that would restrict it to a plain lock.

questions.question: Mutual exclusion can be provided by the __________

options.text: both mutex locks and binary semaphores

questions.explanation:
A mutex is a lock owned by the thread that takes it, and a binary semaphore initialised to 1 and used purely for locking behaves the same way, blocking contenders until the holder signals it. Both constructs therefore provide mutual exclusion, so the combined option applies.

Why C is correct: both mutex locks and binary semaphores provide mutual exclusion.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "mutex locks" is true but names only one of the two mechanisms.
- B: "binary semaphores" is true but names only one of the two mechanisms.
- D: "none" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: When high priority task is indirectly preempted by medium priority task effectively inverting the relative priority of the two tasks, the scenario is called __________
questions.explanation:
Priority inversion occurs when a low-priority task holds a resource that a high-priority task needs, and a medium-priority task preempts the low-priority one so the high-priority task is effectively delayed by a task of lower priority. The usual remedy is the priority-inheritance protocol.

Why A is correct: the scenario is priority inversion.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "priority removal" is not a real term.
- C: "priority exchange" is not a real term.
- D: "priority modification" is not the name of the problem.

questions.question: Process synchronization can be done on __________
questions.explanation:
Mutual exclusion can be enforced by hardware instructions such as test-and-set and compare-and-swap, and equally by purely software algorithms such as Peterson's. Because both approaches work, process synchronisation can be carried out at either level, so the combined option is correct.

Why C is correct: process synchronization can be done at both hardware and software level.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "hardware level" is not the only possible level.
- B: "software level" is not the only possible level.
- D: "none" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: A monitor is a module that encapsulates __________

options.text: procedures that operate on shared data structure

questions.explanation:
A monitor packages the shared data structures, the procedures that operate on that data, and the mutual-exclusion and condition-variable machinery that serialises entry to them. All three of those things are encapsulated inside the monitor construct, so the collective option applies.

Why D is correct: a monitor encapsulates all the listed items.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "shared data structures" is only part of what a monitor encapsulates.
- B: "procedures that operate on shared data structure" is only part of what a monitor encapsulates.
- C: "synchronization between concurrent procedure invocation" is only part of what a monitor encapsulates.

questions.question: To enable a process to wait within the monitor __________

options.text: a condition variable must be declared as condition
condition variables must be used as boolean objects

questions.explanation:
Monitors let a process wait through condition variables, which the programmer declares with the type condition inside the monitor and on which it performs wait and signal. Condition variables are queueing objects rather than boolean flags, and semaphores are a separate primitive that a monitor does not require.

Why A is correct: a condition variable must be declared as condition.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "condition variables must be used as boolean objects" is wrong, they queue processes.
- C: "semaphore must be used" is wrong, semaphores are a separate primitive.
- D: "all" is false because options B and C are wrong.

questions.question: Restricting the child process to a subset of the parent's resources prevents any process from __________

options.text: overloading the system by using a lot of secondary storage
under-loading the system by very less CPU utilization
overloading the system by creating a lot of sub-processes
crashing the system by utilizing multiple resources

questions.explanation:
Without a resource cap, a process that forks children in a loop can spawn an unbounded number of them, and the combined demands of all those sub-processes swamp the machine. Restricting each child to a subset of the parent's resources prevents that kind of system overload.

Why C is correct: it prevents overloading the system by creating a lot of sub-processes.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "overloading the system by using a lot of secondary storage" is not what the restriction targets.
- B: "under-loading the system by very less CPU utilization" describes under-use, not overloading.
- D: "crashing the system by utilizing multiple resources" is wrong, resource caps do not prevent crashes.

questions.question: A parent process calling _____ system call will be suspended until children processes terminate.
questions.explanation:
The wait() call blocks the calling parent until one of its children terminates and then delivers that child's exit status, so it is the call that suspends a parent while its children finish. fork() creates a child, exit() is called by the child, and exec() replaces the calling process image.

Why A is correct: wait() suspends the parent until its children terminate.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "fork" returns immediately after creating the child.
- C: "exit" terminates the calling process, it does not wait for anyone.
- D: "exec" replaces the calling process image with a new program.

questions.question: Cascading termination refers to termination of all child processes if the parent process terminates ______
questions.explanation:
Cascading termination means that when a parent ends, whether it returns normally or is killed abnormally, the system also terminates all of its descendants so no orphaned work continues. It therefore applies to either kind of parent termination.

Why C is correct: cascading termination applies if the parent terminates any one way.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Normally" is too narrow, it also happens on abnormal termination.
- B: "Abnormally" is too narrow, it also happens on normal termination.
- D: "None" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: With _____________ only one process can execute at a time; meanwhile all other process are waiting for the processor. With ______________ more than one process can be running simultaneously each on a different processor.
questions.explanation:
Uniprogramming keeps a single program in memory so only one process executes while all the others wait for the processor. Multiprocessing, by contrast, gives each of several processors its own process so that several run simultaneously on different processors.

Why D is correct: Uniprogramming first, then Multiprocessing.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Uniprogramming, Multiprogramming" is wrong because multiprogramming still uses one CPU, so nothing runs on a different processor.
- B: "Multiprocessing, Multiprogramming" has the two terms in the wrong order.
- C: "Multiprogramming, Multiprocessing" wrongly claims multiprogramming restricts execution to one process.

questions.question: If a process fails, most operating system write the error information to a ______
questions.explanation:
When a process fails the OS usually records the reason in a system log file so an administrator can diagnose the failure after the fact. It does not hand the message to another running process, nor invent an ad-hoc new file on each failure.

Why C is correct: the error information is written to a log file.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "new file" is wrong, a fresh file per failure is not what operating systems do.
- B: "another running process" is wrong, an unrelated process is not given the error.
- D: "none" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: In UNIX, the return value for the fork system call is _____ for the child process and _____ for the parent process.
questions.explanation:
fork() returns 0 in the child, which is how the child recognises itself, and returns the child's PID, a positive non-zero value, in the parent, which is how the parent identifies the new process. A negative return value signals an error and is not tied to either role.

Why C is correct: Zero for the child process and a nonzero integer for the parent.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "A Negative integer, Zero" is reversed, and a negative value means error.
- B: "Zero, A Negative integer" is reversed, the parent gets a positive PID.
- D: "A nonzero integer, Zero" is reversed.

questions.question: The child process can __________

options.text: be a duplicate of the parent process
never be a duplicate of the parent process
cannot have another program loaded into it
never have another program loaded into it

questions.explanation:
fork() gives the child a copy-on-write duplicate of the parent's address space and code, so initially the child is a duplicate of the parent. The child may then call exec() to replace that image with a different program, which is why the claims about never loading another program are also false.

Why A is correct: the child process can be a duplicate of the parent.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "never be a duplicate of the parent process" is false, fork creates exactly that duplicate.
- C: "cannot have another program loaded into it" is false, exec() can replace the child's image.
- D: "never have another program loaded into it" is false for the same reason.

questions.question: The child process completes execution, but the parent keeps executing, then the child process is known as __________
questions.explanation:
After a child exits, its address space is released but its entry in the process table stays until the parent calls wait() and reaps it. Such a terminated but not yet reaped child is called a zombie; an orphan is the opposite case, a child whose parent has already died.

Why B is correct: the child process is known as a Zombie.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Orphan" is a child whose parent has terminated, which is the reverse situation.
- C: "Body" is not a term.
- D: "Dead" is not the defined term.

questions.question: What is Interprocess communication?

options.text: allows processes to communicate and synchronize their actions when using the same address space
allows processes to communicate and synchronize their actions
allows the processes to only synchronize their actions without communication

questions.explanation:
IPC is the activity by which separate processes exchange data and coordinate their relative order of execution, whether by shared memory or by message passing. The definition does not require a shared address space, and it is not limited to synchronisation without data exchange.

Why B is correct: IPC allows processes to communicate and synchronize their actions.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "allows processes to communicate and synchronize their actions when using the same address space" wrongly restricts IPC to a shared address space.
- C: "allows the processes to only synchronize their actions without communication" is wrong, IPC includes communication.
- D: "none" is false, because option B is correct.
questions.reviewReason: extractionFlags mark this as duplicate-stem-of:q_0390, which is also in this shard; both entries were answered independently as instructed.

questions.question: Message passing system allows processes to __________

options.text: communicate with each other without sharing the same address space
communicate with one another by resorting to shared data
name the recipient or sender of the message

questions.explanation:
Message passing gives each process its own private address space and moves data through send and receive operations on a channel or mailbox. That is exactly the alternative to shared memory, in which the participants would have to share one address space.

Why A is correct: message passing lets processes communicate without sharing the same address space.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "communicate with one another by resorting to shared data" describes the shared-memory model.
- C: "share data" is wrong, message passing does not require sharing memory.
- D: "name the recipient or sender of the message" is a property of direct communication, not what message passing enables.

questions.question: Which of the following two operations are provided by the IPC facility?
questions.explanation:
The two primitives every message-passing facility must supply are send(message) and receive(message); without both, a process could neither deposit nor pick up a message. Delete is not one of them, so every option that mentions delete is wrong.

Why D is correct: the facility provides receive and send message.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "write & delete message" includes delete, which is not a message-passing primitive.
- B: "delete & receive message" includes delete, which is not a message-passing primitive.
- C: "send & delete message" includes delete, which is not a message-passing primitive.

questions.question: Messages sent by a process __________

options.text: have to be of a fixed size
have to be a variable size
can be fixed or variable sized

questions.explanation:
Different message-passing designs differ in this respect: some implement a fixed-size message with a single send, while others allow variable-size messages with the receiver supplying a buffer. A message may therefore be either fixed or variable sized depending on the implementation.

Why C is correct: messages can be fixed or variable sized.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "have to be of a fixed size" is wrong, variable-size designs exist.
- B: "have to be a variable size" is wrong, fixed-size designs exist.
- D: "none" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: The link between two processes P and Q to send and receive messages is called __________
questions.explanation:
In the direct, or logical, communication model the connection that lets process P send and Q receive is called a communication link, and it is associated with exactly the two named processes. "Message-passing link" and "synchronization link" are not the terms used for it.

Why A is correct: it is a communication link.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "message-passing link" is not the defined term.
- C: "synchronization link" is not the defined term.
- D: "all" is false, since only option A uses the correct term.

questions.question: Which of the following are TRUE for direct communication?

options.text: A communication link can be associated with N number of process(N = max. number of processes supported by system)
A communication link is associated with exactly two processes
Exactly N/2 links exist between each pair of processes(N = max. number of processes supported by system)
Exactly two link exists between each pair of processes

questions.explanation:
Under direct communication the two processes name each other and a link is set up between exactly that pair, so no link can be shared by N processes. The textbook also notes that the pair is joined by two links, one in each direction, which is what option D states, so this option set admits two readings.

Why B is correct: for direct communication a link is associated with exactly two processes.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "A communication link can be associated with N number of process" describes indirect communication through a shared mailbox.
- C: "Exactly N/2 links exist between each pair of processes" is nonsense, the count does not depend on N.
- D: "Exactly two link exists between each pair of processes" is also stated by the textbook, so the key is ambiguous.
questions.reviewReason: Options B and D are both textbook-true for direct communication (a link is associated with exactly two processes, and exactly two links exist between each pair, one per direction), so the single-answer option set admits two keys.

questions.question: In indirect communication between processes P and Q __________

options.text: there is another process R to handle and pass on the messages between P and Q
there is another machine between the two processes to help communication
there is a mailbox to help communication between P and Q

questions.explanation:
In indirect communication P and Q do not name each other; they both name a shared mailbox or port, deposit messages into it and pick messages out of it. The mailbox is therefore the intermediary that makes the communication possible.

Why C is correct: there is a mailbox to help communication between P and Q.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "there is another process R to handle and pass on the messages" is wrong, no relaying process is involved.
- B: "there is another machine between the two processes" is wrong, indirect communication can happen within one machine.
- D: "none" is false, because option C is correct.

questions.question: Statement 2: The nodes Statement 3: The edges or arcs can be used for transitions Which of the following make the correct combination?
questions.code:
Statement 1: A Finite automata can be represented graphically;
can be its states;

options.text: Statement 1 is false but Statement 2 and 3 are correct
Statement 1 and 2 are correct while 3 is wrong
None of the mentioned statements are correct
All of the mentioned statements are correct

questions.explanation:
The three statements are scattered across the stem and the code field: statement 1, a finite automaton can be represented graphically; statement 2, the nodes can be its states; statement 3, the edges or arcs can be used for transitions. A finite automaton is normally drawn as a transition diagram in which circles (nodes) are states and labelled arrows (arcs) are transitions, so all three are true.

Why D is correct: Each of the three statements describes the standard transition-diagram representation of a finite automaton, so all are correct.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it would require statement 1 to be false, but representing an FA graphically is standard and true.
- B: it would require statement 3 to be false, but labelled arcs are exactly how transitions are drawn.
- C: all three statements hold, so 'none' cannot be the correct combination.
questions.reviewReason: the stem is scrambled: the three statements are split across the question field and the code field ('Statement 1: A Finite automata can be represented graphically' / 'can be its states;'), so the question had to be reconstructed before answering.

questions.question: In a Turing machine the header can move over two cells at the same time
questions.explanation:
A Turing machine performs exactly one move per step: its head moves one cell left, one cell right, or (in some variants) stays where it is while writing a symbol. The transition function delta(q, a) -> (p, b, d) fixes a direction d in {L, R}, so the head always shifts by a single cell and never skips one.

Why B is correct: Each move displaces the head by at most one cell, so moving over two cells at once is impossible.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'true' contradicts the definition of a Turing machine move.
- C: the head displacement is exactly one cell by definition, so no special case exists where it jumps two cells.

questions.question: John is asked to make an deterministic finite automaton which accepts a given string for all the occurrence of '1001' in it. How many number of transitions would John use such that, the string processing application works?
questions.explanation:
A DFA that accepts every string ending in 1001 must remember the longest suffix of the input so far that is also a prefix of 1001, giving the states epsilon, 1, 10, 100 and 1001 (the last one final). Over the binary alphabet each state needs one transition for 0 and one for 1, so 5 x 2 = 10 transitions; building the automaton in code and testing it against all binary strings up to length 5 confirms both the state count and the transition count.

Why A is correct: The minimal suffix-tracking DFA has 5 states with 2 transitions each, i.e. 10 transitions in total.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 11 is impossible because a DFA over Sigma = {0,1} has exactly two transitions per state, so the total must be even.
- C: 12 would need 6 states, but only the 5 prefixes of 1001 have to be distinguished.
- D: 15 is not divisible by 2, so it cannot be the number of transitions of a DFA over a two-symbol alphabet.

questions.question: The production of form -> ε is called:
questions.explanation:
A production A -> epsilon, with A a non-terminal, derives the empty string; such a production is called a null (epsilon) production and exists so that a non-terminal can derive nothing. Sigma is the alphabet of the grammar, while 'null transition' and 'null state' belong to finite automata, so the option that lumps them together cannot be right.

Why B is correct: A -> epsilon derives the empty string, which is exactly what the term null production names.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Sigma denotes the alphabet, not a type of production.
- C: a null state is an automata concept (a state with no outgoing transitions).
- D: it would require Sigma and null state to name this production, and neither does.

questions.question: The number of tuples in an Non Deterministic Finite Automaton:
questions.explanation:
An NFA is the 5-tuple M = (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F): the state set Q, the input alphabet Sigma, the transition function delta, the start state q0 and the set F of final states. Nondeterminism changes what delta returns (a set of states, possibly empty) but not the number of components, so the tuple has five fields.

Why A is correct: Q, Sigma, delta, q0 and F are the five components of the standard finite automaton tuple.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: a finite automaton has five components, not six.
- C: seven fields would describe a transducer or Mealy/Moore machine, which adds an output alphabet.
- D: four fields would drop either the start state or the final-state set, both of which are required.

questions.question: Predict the number of transitions required to build a DFA for the following language using only 3
questions.code:
states: ∑{0,1}
L= {w | w ends with 00}
questions.explanation:
The language {w | w ends with 00} over Sigma = {0,1} needs three states: no trailing zero, exactly one trailing zero, and two or more trailing zeros (final). A DFA transition function is total, so each of the three states must define a move for both 0 and 1, giving 3 x 2 = 6 transitions; running the constructed automaton over all binary strings up to length 6 confirms it accepts exactly the strings ending in 00.

Why A is correct: With only three states over a two-symbol alphabet the total transition function has 3 x 2 = 6 entries.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 3 would be one transition per state, impossible for a total function over a two-symbol alphabet.
- C: 4 is below the minimum of 6 entries that three states require.
- D: the count is fully determined by |Q| x |Sigma| = 3 x 2, so it can be stated.

questions.question: In NFA a state cannot travel to more than one state using the same input symbol
questions.explanation:
In an NFA the transition function is a relation: delta(q, a) is a set of states, so a single state may have several successors for the same input symbol, and epsilon-moves are allowed as well. Restricting a state to exactly one successor per symbol is precisely what makes the automaton deterministic.

Why B is correct: Multiple successors for the same state and symbol is exactly the feature that makes an automaton non-deterministic.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'true' is the opposite of the definition; this restriction holds for a DFA, not for an NFA.

questions.question: In the tuples which is used to represent an automata Q represents the states in the automata
questions.explanation:
The automaton tuple M = (Q, Sigma, delta, q0, F) uses Q for the finite set of states of the machine. The remaining fields name the alphabet, the transition function, the start state and the final states, so Q is exactly the state set.

Why A is correct: Q is the component of the tuple that denotes the set of states.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: the tuple's Q field is precisely the state set, so the statement is not false.

questions.question: In the tuples which is used to represent an automata, F represents the non final state elements in the automata
questions.explanation:
F in the automaton tuple denotes the set of final (accepting) states, that is the states in which the machine accepts the input. The non-final states are simply the complement Q minus F, so describing F as the non-final elements reverses its meaning.

Why B is correct: F holds the final states, not the non-final ones, so the claim is false.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'true' would require F to be the set of non-final states, which contradicts the definition of F.

questions.question: All DFA's can be called as NFA's
questions.explanation:
Every DFA is a special case of an NFA, because an NFA permits zero, one or many successors per symbol and a DFA always has exactly one. Since a DFA therefore also satisfies the definition of an NFA, all DFAs may be called NFAs, while the reverse inclusion fails.

Why A is correct: DFA is a strict subset of NFA, so each DFA is also a valid NFA.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: the inclusion runs the other way; an NFA with several successors for one symbol is not a DFA.

questions.question: Kleen closure property is represented with * symbol
questions.explanation:
Kleene closure, written with the postfix star, means zero or more repetitions of the preceding expression, so (a+b)* contains epsilon, a, b, aa, ab and so on. The plus sign, not the star, is the operator for one-or-more repetition.

Why A is correct: The postfix '*' is the standard symbol for Kleene closure in regular expressions.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: the statement gives standard notation, so 'false' is incorrect.

questions.question: Alphabet set is formed using symbols

options.text: May not be true in all cases
May be false in some cases

questions.explanation:
An alphabet is by definition a finite, non-empty set of symbols, so it is built out of symbols, exactly as Sigma = {0,1} shows. There is no case in which an alphabet is made of anything other than symbols.

Why A is correct: Sigma is a set of symbols, which is the definition of an alphabet.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: an alphabet can be nothing but a set of symbols.
- C: no exception exists in the formal definition, so 'may not be true in all cases' is wrong.
- D: the claim that it may be false in some cases contradicts the definition.

questions.question: Positive closure represented with *
questions.explanation:
Positive closure means one or more repetitions and is written with the postfix '+', as in (a+b)+, which excludes the empty string. The star '*' denotes Kleene closure, zero or more repetitions, so the statement swaps the two operators.

Why B is correct: Positive closure uses '+', while '*' is Kleene (zero-or-more) closure.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'true' would make '*' the positive-closure operator, but '*' also allows zero repetitions.

questions.question: In a Context Free Grammar every Terminal produces a language
questions.explanation:
In a context free grammar every non-terminal (variable) defines a language, namely the set of terminal strings derivable from it, while each terminal is a single literal symbol with no derivation of its own. Attaching the languages to the terminals therefore reverses the roles.

Why B is correct: Languages belong to non-terminals, so a terminal does not produce a language.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'true' would mean every terminal generates a language, but terminals are leaves of the parse tree.

questions.question: The formal notation of a context free grammar is
questions.explanation:
A context free grammar is written G = (V, T, P, S) or equivalently G = {V, T, P, S}, where V is the set of non-terminals, T the set of terminals, P the set of productions and S the start symbol. Omitting S, P or V leaves the grammar incomplete, and G1 is not a component of the notation.

Why A is correct: The four components V, T, P and S are exactly the fields listed in G = {V, T, P, S}.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: omits the start symbol S, which every CFG must have.
- C: omits the production set P, which is the grammar itself.
- D: G1 is not a component; the grammar is named by G outside the braces.

questions.question: A variable non terminal may be __________ if there is no way of getting terminal from it.
questions.explanation:
A non-terminal is useless when it cannot derive any terminal string, or cannot be reached from the start symbol; deleting it together with all its productions leaves L(G) unchanged. A variable from which no terminal can ever be derived is exactly that definition.

Why B is correct: If no terminal string is derivable from the variable, it is useless and can be removed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'useful' is the opposite of what the stated condition describes.
- C: whatever the decidability, the accepted term for a variable that yields no terminal string is useless.

questions.question: which of the following grammar are useless productions S→aS | A | C A→a B→aa C→aCb

options.text: S→aS | A | C A→a B→aa C→aCb

questions.explanation:
A production is useless when it can never take part in a derivation of a terminal string from S. Checking each option by computing which non-terminals are generating and which are reachable from S: in A the rule C -> aCb only ever yields a^n C b^n, so C never derives a terminal and the production S -> C is useless (and B is also unreachable from S); in B the symbol C has no production at all; in C both A and C are undefined; in D, C -> aCb never terminates and B is unreachable from S. All four options therefore contain useless symbols, so the item is defective, and A is recorded because it is exactly the grammar printed in the stem.

Why A is correct: In this grammar C -> aCb can only produce a^n C b^n, which never reduces to terminals, so S -> C is a useless production.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: C is produced by S -> C but has no production, so this option also contains a useless symbol.
- C: A and C occur in S's productions without any definition, so they are useless too.
- D: C -> aCb never yields terminals and B is unreachable from S, so this option is useless as well.
questions.reviewReason: all four options contain useless symbols or productions (verified by computing generating/reachable non-terminals), so the question has no unique correct option; option A was chosen only because it is the grammar that the extraction also printed inside the stem.

questions.question: A grammar is said to be ambiguous when

options.text: if there exists some w∈L(G) which has atleast two left most or right most derivations
if there exists some w∈L(G) which has atleast one left most or right most derivations
if there exists some w∈L(G) which no left most or right most derivations

questions.explanation:
A grammar is ambiguous when some string w in L(G) admits two or more distinct derivations, equivalently two distinct parse trees. The standard example S -> S + S | 1 derives the string 1+1+1 in two different leftmost ways, which is exactly the situation the option describes.

Why A is correct: The existence of a w in L(G) with at least two leftmost (or rightmost) derivations is the definition of ambiguity.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: every string of L(G) has at least one derivation in any grammar, so this says nothing about ambiguity.
- C: a string of L(G) with no derivation at all would not belong to L(G).
- D: 'all' cannot hold since B and C are not definitions of ambiguity.

questions.question: Any production of a context free grammar of the form A→B where A,B∈V is called
questions.explanation:
A production whose left and right sides are single non-terminals, A -> B with A, B in V, contributes no terminals and is called a unit production; such rules can be eliminated when a grammar is simplified. It is neither a useless symbol (both symbols may be perfectly useful) nor a null production, which has the form A -> epsilon.

Why A is correct: A -> B with both sides non-terminals is exactly the definition of a unit production.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: a unit production may involve useful non-terminals, so it is not a useless symbol.
- C: a null production has the form A -> epsilon, not A -> B.
- D: 'all' would require the production to be a useless symbol and a null production as well.

questions.question: where V represents Terminals
questions.code: In G{V,T,P,S}
questions.explanation:
In G = {V, T, P, S} the letter V stands for variables, that is non-terminals, and T stands for the terminal alphabet. The statement assigns the terminals to V and is therefore false; there is no alternative reading of the notation.

Why B is correct: V is the non-terminal (variable) set and T is the terminal set, so the claim is false.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'true' would require V to be the terminal set, but terminals are denoted by T.
- C: the notation fixes V as the variables, with no case in which it means terminals.

questions.question: A grammar G is called a CFG if production has

options.text: any combination of terminals and non-terminals on its RHS
only one terminal in LHS and any combination of terminals and non-terminals on its RHS

questions.explanation:
The defining restriction of a context free grammar is the shape of a production: the left-hand side is a single non-terminal and the right-hand side is an arbitrary string of terminals and non-terminals, epsilon included. Both conditions are needed, which is what option D states, although its wording says 'terminal in LHS' where it should read 'non-terminal'.

Why D is correct: Only D carries both halves of the CFG condition, a single non-terminal on the left and any mix of terminals and non-terminals on the right.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: a CFG left-hand side must be a non-terminal, not a terminal, and this option also omits the RHS condition.
- B: it constrains only the right side and says nothing about the left side.
- C: the right side of a CFG production may begin with anything, including a terminal.
questions.reviewReason: options A and D say 'terminal in LHS' where the CFG condition requires a non-terminal; the intended key is D (it is the only option stating both conditions) but the printed wording is technically wrong.

questions.question: Which of the following grammar is ambiguous
questions.explanation:
Counting distinct leftmost derivations (parse trees) for each grammar shows that S -> aS | Sa | a is ambiguous, since the string aa has the two derivations S => aS => aa and S => Sa => aa, and that S -> S0S0S | 1 is ambiguous too, since strings such as 101010101 have several parse trees, while S -> 0S0 | 1S1 | 0 | 1 | epsilon has exactly one parse tree per generated string and is unambiguous. Two options are therefore ambiguous and the item has no unique key; C is recorded as the likely intended answer.

Why C is correct: With S -> S0S0S | 1 the string 101010101 can be split among the inner S symbols in more than one way, giving several distinct parse trees.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: S -> aS | Sa | a is also ambiguous because aa has the two leftmost derivations above, which makes the option set defective.
- B: S -> 0S0 | 1S1 | 0 | 1 | epsilon has exactly one parse tree for every generated string, so it is unambiguous.
- D: 'All of these' fails because option B is unambiguous.
questions.reviewReason: two options are correct: both A (S->aS|Sa|a, witness 'aa') and C (S->S0S0S|1, witness '101010101') are ambiguous, verified by counting parse trees, so the key must be checked against the source.

questions.question: Languages are conditions in forming strings over the symbols available in the alphabet set

options.text: may be true in some cases
may be false in most of the cases

questions.explanation:
A language over an alphabet Sigma is a subset of Sigma*, so it is exactly a condition that selects which of the strings formed from the symbols of Sigma belong to it. That is why a language is described as the set of strings over a given alphabet satisfying some stated property.

Why A is correct: Formally a language is a set of strings over Sigma satisfying a given condition, which is a condition on how strings are formed.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: the sentence is the standard informal definition of a language.
- C: it holds for every language, so 'may be true in some cases' understates it.
- D: no language fails to restrict the strings formed from its alphabet.

questions.question: The CFG for the language L={0^n 1^n |n>=1} is
questions.explanation:
With S -> 0S1 | 01 each application of the recursive rule wraps one more 0 on the left and one more 1 on the right of a base string 01, so the grammar generates exactly 0^n 1^n for n >= 1 and nothing else; generating the language and comparing it against the target for all lengths up to 16 gives no extra and no missing strings. The other grammars clearly overshoot: S -> 0S | S0 | 1 also produces 00000010 and 0000010, S -> 0S0 | 1S1 | 0 | 1 | epsilon is the mirror language and produces 00100, and S -> S0S0S | 1 produces 10101.

Why D is correct: S -> 0S1 | 01 yields 01, 0011, 000111 and so on, which is precisely {0^n 1^n | n >= 1}.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: S -> 0S | S0 | 1 generates strings such as 0000010 that are not of the form 0^n 1^n.
- B: S -> 0S0 | 1S1 | 0 | 1 | epsilon generates 00100 and 0001000, which contain a trailing block of zeros.
- C: S -> S0S0S | 1 generates 10101, which is not of the form 0^n 1^n.

questions.question: Which of the following machines accepts regular languages
questions.explanation:
Finite automata are exactly the machines that recognise the regular languages, and both the DFA and the NFA accept precisely the regular languages. A PDA recognises the context free languages, a strictly larger class. Because an NFA accepts exactly the same regular languages as a DFA, and because every regular language is also context free, the option set here admits more than one defensible reading.

Why B is correct: The DFA is the standard machine model defined as recognising exactly the regular languages, so it is the conventional answer.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: an NFA accepts the same regular languages, so the option is defensible too, which is why the item is flagged.
- C: a PDA recognises context free languages, which includes non-regular ones such as a^n b^n.
- D: as written, a PDA can also be built to accept any regular language, so 'All' is not cleanly excluded.
questions.reviewReason: the option set has more than one defensible answer: NFA accepts exactly the regular languages as well, and since regular is a subset of context free a PDA can accept them too, so 'All' is also arguable; B is the conventional key.

questions.question: Which of the following languages can be accepted by DPDA
questions.explanation:
The option reads W c W^R with W in {a,b}*, the language of a's and b's placed around a central marker c. A DPDA pushes each symbol of the first half, and when it reaches the unique marker c it switches to the matching phase and pops one stack symbol per remaining input symbol, accepting when the input and the stack run out together, so no guess is ever needed. In contrast a^n b^n requires the machine to guess how many a's to match with b's, which is why no DPDA accepts it.

Why A is correct: The centre marker c makes the middle of the string unambiguous, so W c W^R is deterministic context free and a DPDA accepts it.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: a^n b^n is the standard non-deterministic context free language, accepted only by an NPDA.
- C: 'both are correct' fails because a^n b^n is not accepted by any DPDA.
- D: 'both are wrong' fails because W c W^R is accepted by a DPDA.

questions.question: which of the following languages are accepted by NPDA but not by DPDA
questions.explanation:
A language accepted by an NPDA but not by a DPDA is context free yet not deterministic, because the machine must guess something it cannot determine from the input. Palindromes are exactly that case: the PDA has to locate the middle of the string, and no deterministic rule can do it, so an NPDA guesses the halfway point while no DPDA exists. The other options are deterministic: for m = n the machine pushes on 0, pops on 1, ignores 2 and accepts when the stack empties, which is a DPDA, and option C as printed writes 2^m while constraining m = n + p, which forces n = 0 and leaves the regular language 0^m 2^m.

Why A is correct: An NPDA accepts all palindromes by guessing the halfway point, and no DPDA can, because the machine cannot decide deterministically whether to push the next symbol or to match it.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: m = n is enforced deterministically by popping one symbol per 1 and accepting when the stack is empty, so this is a DCFL.
- C: as printed the third block is 2^m while the condition is m = n + p, which forces n = 0 and gives the regular language {0^m 2^m}.
- D: 'none' is wrong because even-length palindromes are a genuine NPDA-only example.
questions.reviewReason: option C is internally inconsistent as printed ({0^m 1^n 2^m with the condition m = n + p leaves p unused and reduces to the regular language {0^m 2^m}); the key A rests on even-length palindromes requiring the nondeterministic halfway-point guess.

questions.question: PDA is equivalent to finite automata except that it has an extra memory unit called as queue
questions.explanation:
The extra memory of a PDA is a stack, which is last-in-first-out: only the most recently pushed symbol can be inspected or removed. A queue is first-in-first-out, so calling that unit a queue misdescribes the model; a machine with a queue is a different, more powerful kind of automaton.

Why B is correct: The auxiliary memory of a PDA is a stack (LIFO), not a queue (FIFO).

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'true' would require the PDA's memory to be a queue, which the model does not use.

questions.question: Finite state machines have limited memory only in the form of states.
questions.explanation:
A finite state machine has no auxiliary storage at all; its only memory is the control state it currently occupies. Having to encode the relevant history into the finite state set is exactly why finite automata recognise only the regular languages.

Why A is correct: The entire memory of a finite state machine is the set of its states and which one it is in.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'false' would require memory outside the states, but the model has none.

questions.question: PDA may be deterministic or non-deterministic.
questions.explanation:
Both variants of the PDA model exist: a deterministic PDA allows at most one move per configuration, while a non-deterministic PDA may branch, which is what lets it accept languages such as a^n b^n and w w^R. Nondeterminism is strictly more powerful here, and both models are standard.

Why A is correct: DPDA and NPDA are both recognised PDA variants, and the nondeterministic one is strictly more powerful.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'false' would deny the non-deterministic variant, which is a standard and widely used PDA model.

questions.question: In formal notation Z0 is stack bottom symbol
questions.explanation:
The transition function of a PDA is written delta(q, a, X) where X is the stack symbol on top, and Z0 is the distinguished symbol placed in the initial stack. It marks the bottom of the stack and lets the machine detect that the stack has become empty.

Why A is correct: Z0 is by convention the bottom-of-stack (initial stack) symbol of a PDA.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: the statement matches the standard notation for the PDA transition function, so it is not false.

questions.question: which of the following language is not regular
questions.explanation:
Regular languages are exactly those recognised by finite automata. The set {a^n | n >= 0} is matched by a one-state DFA with a self loop, and {a^2n | n >= 0} needs only two states that track an even or odd number of a's, so A and C are regular; option B, read as {a^n b^n | n >= 0}, is the classic language that no finite automaton can recognise because it must compare the counts of two different symbols.

Why B is correct: a^n b^n requires matching counts of two different symbols, which no finite automaton can track, so it is not regular.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: {a^n | n >= 0} is simply a* and is regular.
- C: {a^2n | n >= 0} is the even number of a's, recognised by a two-state DFA.
- D: 'all' fails because A and C are regular.
questions.reviewReason: option B is printed as 'L={a^n*n | n>=0}', which is not a valid language definition; read as {a^n b^n | n >= 0} it is the only non-regular option, but as printed the item has no well-defined non-regular option.

questions.question: If the PDA does not stop on an accepting state and the stack is not empty, the string is:
questions.explanation:
A PDA accepts a string only when the computation halts in an accepting configuration: with the final-state convention it must halt in a final state, and with the empty-stack convention the stack must be emptied. If the machine halts without reaching an accepting state and the stack still holds symbols, neither condition is satisfied, so the string is rejected.

Why A is correct: Acceptance requires an accepting configuration, so halting elsewhere with a non-empty stack is a rejection.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'accepted' would require an accepting state or an empty stack, neither of which holds.
- C: 'all of the mentioned' cannot hold because accepted and rejected are opposite outcomes.
- D: 'none of the mentioned' is wrong since the string is indeed rejected.

questions.question: Strings can have symbols which are not shown in the alphabet set
questions.explanation:
A string over an alphabet Sigma is by definition a finite sequence of symbols drawn from Sigma, so every symbol it contains must be a member of Sigma. A sequence containing a symbol outside the alphabet is simply not a string of that language.

Why B is correct: Sigma* contains only sequences built from the symbols of Sigma, so no outside symbol can appear.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'yes' contradicts the definition of a string over an alphabet.
- C: there is no special case; the alphabet fixes the permitted symbols completely.

questions.question: The operations of PDA never work on elements, other than the top symbol in stack.
questions.explanation:
A PDA may read and modify only the symbol at the top of its stack; anything below it stays unreachable until the symbols above it have been popped. This LIFO restriction is exactly what gives the PDA context free power, and it is why languages such as a^n b^n force nondeterminism.

Why A is correct: Every PDA operation inspects and rewrites only the stack top, never an element deeper in the stack.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'FALSE' would require the PDA to reach stack elements below the top, which the model does not allow.

questions.question: Languages determine the nature of string formed using the given alphabet set
questions.explanation:
A language is a subset of Sigma* selected by a stated property, so it fixes which of the strings formed from the alphabet's symbols are admitted and which are not. Saying that a language determines the nature of the strings formed from a given alphabet set is a restatement of that definition.

Why A is correct: A language is precisely the condition that decides which strings over the alphabet belong to it.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'no' contradicts the definition of a language as a set of strings over Sigma.
- C: the statement is true for every language, not merely in some cases.

questions.question: Identify the string set for the Σ {0,1}∗ even count of zeros and even count of ones
questions.explanation:
The language is all binary strings with an even number of 0s and an even number of 1s; the empty string has zero of each, so it must belong because the closure shown is Sigma*, not Sigma+. Checking every listed member of B gives epsilon (0 zeros, 0 ones), 00 (2,0), 11 (0,2), 0101 (2,2) and 00001111 (4,4), all of which qualify, whereas C's 010, 101, 001 and 0000111 each contain an odd number of 1s.

Why B is correct: B includes epsilon, which is in Sigma* and has even counts of both symbols, and every other member it lists satisfies the parity condition.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it omits epsilon, which is in the language because the closure is Sigma* and contains the empty string.
- C: 010, 101, 001 and 0000111 all have an odd number of 1s, so they are not in the language.
- D: wrong, because B does give the correct string set.

The stem is empty in the source and the statement was extracted into the code field as Sigma {0,1}^3 = {000, 001, 010, 011, 100, 101, 110, 111}, i.e. the third power of the binary alphabet. Generating that set gives exactly the 2^3 = 8 binary strings of length three, with nothing missing and nothing extra, so the stated equality is correct.

Why A is correct: {0,1}^3 contains exactly the eight binary strings of length three, which are precisely the eight strings listed.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'wrong' would require a missing or an extra string, and the generated set matches the listed set element for element.
questions.reviewReason: extractionFlags show an empty stem: the question text was lost and only the code field carries the statement, which had to be read as the third power of the binary alphabet before it could be judged true or false.

questions.question: Identify the string set for the Σ {0,1}+ even count of zeros and odd count of ones
questions.explanation:
The target language is the non-empty binary strings with an even number of 0s and an odd number of 1s. Testing each candidate set shows that D contains only valid strings: 001 (2 zeros, 1 one), 100 (2,1), 0000111 (4,3) and 10101 (2,3). Every other option has a counterexample, with A including epsilon which has zero (an even number of) 1s and is excluded by Sigma+ as well, B including 01 which has a single 0, and C including 0101, 1010 and 1001 which each have two 1s plus 101001 which has three 0s.

Why D is correct: Every string listed in D has an even count of 0s and an odd count of 1s, and no string outside the language appears.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it lists epsilon, which is not in Sigma+ and has an even (zero) number of 1s.
- B: it lists 01, which has a single 0 and hence an odd number of zeros.
- C: it lists 0101, 1010 and 1001, all of which have two 1s (even), and 101001, which has three 0s (odd).

questions.question: In DFA, a state cannot travel to more than one state with the same input symbol
questions.explanation:
Determinism means that for every state q and input symbol a the transition function gives exactly one next state, so delta is a function rather than a relation. If a state could reach two different states with the same input symbol, the machine would be an NFA instead.

Why A is correct: In a DFA every state has exactly one outgoing transition per input symbol.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'false' is the defining property of an NFA, not of a DFA.
- C: the restriction holds in every DFA, not merely in some cases.

questions.question: In memory transfer location address is supplied by____ that puts this on address bus
questions.explanation:
Every CPU to memory transfer starts by loading the address of the target word into a dedicated register whose only job is to drive the address bus, and that register is the memory address register (MAR). The MAR is wired directly to the address bus and holds the address stable for the whole read or write cycle, while the data word travels on the separate data bus through the MDR. The ALU computes addresses but is never connected to the address bus, and the CPU as a whole supplies the address only indirectly, through its MAR.

Why C is correct: The MAR holds the address of the memory location and is the register whose output is placed on the address bus.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: The ALU only computes addresses and is not connected to the address bus.
- B: The CPU produces the address through its MAR; the CPU itself is not the register that drives the bus.
- D: The MDR (data register) sits on the data bus and carries the data word, not the address.
questions.reviewReason: The published key for this item in the source question bank is CPU, but the register that puts the address on the address bus is unambiguously the MAR; answered as printed using standard theory.

questions.question: Control memory is part of ______ that has addressable storage registers and used as temporary storage for data
questions.explanation:
Control memory is the control store of a microprogrammed control unit, holding the microinstructions that drive the datapath. The relative clause in the stem, "that has addressable storage registers and used as temporary storage for data", is the textbook description of random access memory, so the blank is RAM on the wording of the source text. Note that mainstream textbooks instead present the control store as a read only memory inside the CPU, which is why this item is flagged.

Why B is correct: RAM is random access memory made of addressable storage locations and used as temporary storage for data, exactly as the stem describes.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: ROM is read only, so it cannot serve as temporary storage for data as the stem requires.
- C: The CPU does contain the control unit, but a CPU is not described as addressable storage registers used for temporary data storage.
- D: "Memory" is too general; the stem's wording points specifically at random access memory.
questions.reviewReason: Stem is garbled and contradicts standard theory (control memory/control store is normally a ROM inside the CPU); the source text defines control memory as a RAM of addressable storage registers, which is why RAM was chosen.

questions.question: How many modes the address in control memory are divided into?
questions.explanation:
The address space of control memory is split into two groups, a task mode and an executive (interrupt) mode, each addressed through its own address select logic. So the number of modes the control memory address is divided into is two. This is confirmed by the companion item in the same bank, whose answer choice is "Both Executive mode & Task Mode", which implies exactly two modes.

Why A is correct: The control memory addresses are divided into two groups, the task mode and the executive (interrupt) mode.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Three address modes do not exist for control memory.
- C: Five is the maximum number of register groups inside control memory, not the number of address modes.
- D: Seven is not a count that occurs anywhere in the control memory address scheme.

questions.question: which of the following is interrupt mode
questions.explanation:
Control memory addresses are divided into a task mode and an executive mode, and the executive mode is explicitly the interrupt mode, used for the control storage that serves interrupt handling while the task mode serves normal programmed operation. Since the question asks which of the listed modes is the interrupt mode, the executive mode is the answer.

Why B is correct: The executive mode is the interrupt mode group of control memory addresses.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Task mode is the other address group, used for ordinary programmed CPU operation rather than interrupts.
- C: Both are control memory modes, but only the executive mode carries the interrupt label.
- D: A defined mode does exist, namely the executive mode.

questions.question: Mode of addresses in control memory are:
questions.explanation:
The mode of addressing control memory is split into two groups, the task mode and the executive (interrupt) mode. Because both of the listed modes exist, the correct choice is the option that accepts both. This matches the companion item in the same bank, which records two modes as the count.

Why C is correct: Both the executive mode and the task mode are the two modes of addressing control memory.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Executive mode alone is incomplete, the task mode group also exists.
- B: Task mode alone is incomplete, the executive (interrupt) group also exists.
- D: Incorrect, both modes are named in the definition of control memory addressing.

questions.question: On what method search in cache memory used by the system
questions.explanation:
When a processor with a cache issues a memory reference, the address is generated and the cache is searched to see whether a copy is held there. The way that search is carried out depends on the cache mapping technique the system uses, that is whether the cache is direct mapped, set associative or fully associative. Of the four choices, only cache mapping names that technique.

Why B is correct: The method used to search the cache depends on the type of cache mapping employed by the computer system.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: "Cache directing" is not a recognised cache technique.
- C: "Cache controlling" refers to the control logic around the cache, not to how a requested address is searched for.
- D: Cache invalidation is one of the three areas of the cache process (it writes only to the directory to remove an entry), not the search method.

questions.question: Microprograms are usually stored in
questions.explanation:
A microprogram is the ordered set of microinstructions that implements the machine instruction set of a microprogrammed control unit, and it is held in the control store. That store is normally a read only memory so the microcode cannot be changed by ordinary operation or by a stray write, which is why microprograms are usually stored in ROM.

Why A is correct: Microprograms are normally kept in the read only control store, a ROM, so the microcode remains fixed.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: RAM is volatile and writable, so it is used only when the control store is deliberately writable (dynamic microprogramming), not the usual case.
- C: SAM (semiconductor access memory) is a telecommunications memory term and is never used for microprograms.
- D: SAN (storage area network) is a networking concept with no role in control storage.

questions.question: In which addressing the operand is actually present in instruction
questions.explanation:
In immediate addressing the data operand itself is coded into the instruction word, so the processor needs no further memory or register reference to obtain it. This is the only mode in which the operand, rather than a reference to it, appears inside the instruction.

Why A is correct: With immediate addressing the operand value is actually present in the instruction itself.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: In direct addressing only the address of the operand is in the instruction; the operand must still be fetched from memory.
- C: In register addressing the operand is held in a register selected by a field of the instruction.
- D: Incorrect, one of the listed modes is the correct answer.

questions.question: In which addressing the simplest addressing mode where an operand is fetched from memory is_____
questions.explanation:
Direct (absolute) addressing is the simplest of the modes in which the operand is fetched from memory, because the address field of the instruction is used as the effective address with no register, displacement or indexing added. The operand therefore comes straight from the memory location named in the instruction.

Why B is correct: Direct addressing uses the instruction address field as the effective address, so the operand is fetched directly from memory.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Immediate addressing takes the operand from inside the instruction, not from memory.
- C: Register addressing takes the operand from a processor register, not from memory.
- D: Incorrect, one of the listed modes is the correct answer.

questions.question: which addressing is a way of direct addressing
questions.explanation:
The stem is circular, asking which addressing is a way of direct addressing, so it can only be answered as printed. Answered that way, direct addressing is the mode in which the address field of the instruction is the effective address of the operand itself, with no pointer or index involved, and that is the option chosen.

Why B is correct: Direct addressing is the mode in which the address given in the instruction is used as the effective address of the operand.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Immediate addressing places the operand itself in the instruction, so it is not a way of direct addressing.
- C: Register addressing names a register rather than using the address in the instruction.
- D: Incorrect, direct addressing is one of the listed options.
questions.reviewReason: Stem is tautological/garbled ("which addressing is a way of direct addressing"); answered B as printed, which is the only option consistent with the wording.

questions.question: In which mode the main memory location holds the Effective Address of the operand
questions.explanation:
Indirect addressing is the mode in which the address field of the instruction points to a memory location whose content is the effective address of the operand. That is the distinguishing feature described in the stem, a main memory location holding the effective address, and it costs one extra memory reference compared with direct addressing.

Why D is correct: In indirect addressing the effective address of the operand is held in a main memory location pointed to by the instruction.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Immediate addressing keeps the operand in the instruction, so no address is stored in memory at all.
- B: Direct addressing uses the instruction address field itself, with nothing stored in memory to be dereferenced.
- C: Register addressing keeps the address in a processor register, not in a main memory location.

questions.question: Operation of memory transfer are
questions.explanation:
Memory transfer covers both directions of traffic between the CPU and memory. A read moves a word from a memory location into the processor, and a write moves a word from the processor into a memory location, so the set of memory transfer operations is read and write together.

Why C is correct: The memory transfer operations are read and write, so both are required.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: Read is only one direction of memory transfer; the write operation is the other.
- B: Write is only one direction of memory transfer; the read operation is the other.
- D: Incorrect, read and write are both genuine memory transfer operations.

questions.question: Which addressing is an extremely influential way of addressing
questions.explanation:
Displacement addressing forms the effective address by adding a displacement to a base register, an index register or the program counter. It is the most influential mode in practice because it is what lets one instruction reach an element of an array, a stack frame or a structure, all of which need an address that is computed at run time. Immediate, direct and register addressing are all simpler but cannot express such a computed address.

Why A is correct: Displacement addressing, by adding a displacement to a register or the PC, is the influential mode that makes arrays, stacks and structures addressable.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: Immediate addressing cannot reach beyond the instruction word.
- C: Direct addressing needs a full address field in every instruction, so its range and code density are poor.
- D: Register addressing operates on a register and never names a memory operand.

questions.question: Which algorithm is a multiplication algorithm which multiplies two signed binary numbers in 2's complement notation
questions.explanation:
Multiplying two signed binary numbers held in 2's complement requires that the sign be handled arithmetically rather than stripped off first. Booth's algorithm does this by recoding the multiplier bits as M+1, M or M-1 so that the whole signed product is formed with additions and arithmetic shifts only. The usual shift and add multiplier, by contrast, is defined on unsigned magnitudes.

Why B is correct: Booth's multiplication algorithm is the algorithm that multiplies two signed binary numbers in 2's complement notation.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: The usual multiplication algorithm is the plain shift and add multiplier for unsigned values, and is not the 2's complement signed algorithm.
- C: The usual multiplier is not the signed 2's complement algorithm, so "Both" is wrong.
- D: Incorrect, Booth's algorithm exists and is the standard signed multiplier.

questions.question: . ________interrupt establishes a priority over the various sources to determine which request should be entertained first
questions.explanation:
When several devices can raise an interrupt at the same time, the hardware needs a rule for deciding which request is serviced first. A priority interrupt scheme assigns each source a priority level so that the highest priority pending request is entertained first, and the blank in the stem is followed by the word interrupt, so the phrase must end in "interrupt".

Why A is correct: A priority interrupt establishes a priority over the various sources to determine which request should be entertained first.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: "Polling interrupt" is not a scheme; polling is a software technique that queries devices in turn and establishes no priority among them.
- C: "Daisy chaining interrupt" is not a term; daisy chaining is one physical wiring technique for a fixed priority, not the generic scheme described.
- D: Incorrect, a defined term exists and it is priority interrupt.

questions.question: An instruction code must specify the address of the____
questions.explanation:
An instruction has two logical parts, an opcode field that names the operation and an address field that identifies the operand. As well as saying what to do, the instruction must therefore say where the operand is, by giving its address directly or by giving the information needed to compute it, otherwise the operation could not be carried out.

Why B is correct: An instruction code must specify the address of the operand on which the operation is to be performed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: The opcode names the operation itself and says nothing about a location in memory.
- C: The opcode and the address field are separate parts of the instruction; only the address field specifies the operand.
- D: Incorrect, the address of the operand is one of the things an instruction code must specify.

questions.question: In memory, the read operation puts memory address on to a register known as
questions.explanation:
A memory read is started by putting the address of the wanted word into the memory address register, whose output is wired to the address bus, and then asserting the read control line; the word returns on the data bus into the MDR. The register that receives the address for this purpose is the MAR, while the PC only ever supplies the address of the next instruction.

Why C is correct: The MAR is the register that holds the memory address and puts it on to the address bus for the read.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: The PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched, it is not the register driving the address bus for a memory read.
- B: The ALU performs arithmetic and logic and is not the register that drives the address bus.
- D: Incorrect, only the MAR holds the address placed on the bus, so "All of these" is false.

questions.question: Which operation puts memory address in memory address register and data in DR
questions.explanation:
In a memory write cycle the CPU itself loads both halves of the transfer before the cycle starts: the address of the destination word goes into the memory address register and the data word goes into the data register, and only then is the write signal asserted so the memory latches the word. In a read the CPU loads only the address, and the data word arrives from memory into the data register rather than being put there by the CPU, which is the distinction the stem relies on.

Why B is correct: In a memory write the CPU puts the address in the MAR and the data in the DR before the write cycle begins.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: In a memory read the data is delivered by memory into the DR, the CPU does not put it there.
- C: "Both" can also be defended, since a read uses the MAR and the DR too, which is why this item is flagged for review.
- D: Incorrect, memory write is a defined memory transfer operation.
questions.reviewReason: Genuinely ambiguous: in a memory read the address also goes into the MAR and the returned data lands in the DR, so option C (Both) is defensible as well as B; answered B as the published key has it.

questions.question: The memory bus is also referred as______
questions.explanation:
